1. Do NOT restart prednisone or other steroids now; atypical CT is not typical immune pneumonitis (usually ground-glass/organizing pneumonia) and steroids will worsen TB/NTM/fungal disease.
2. Urgently assess severity with vitals, pulse oximetry at rest and with ambulation, lung exam, and compare to prior CTs; obtain 3 sputum samples (induced if needed) for AFB smear, mycobacterial culture, and Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra NAAT, plus sputum bacterial culture; send HIV Ag/Ab, CBC, CMP; retrieve records of LTBI evaluation/treatment from 5 years ago and ask about TB contacts, travel/birthplace, gardening/soil, hot tub, birds, smoking, current cancer therapy, diabetes, and prior PJP prophylaxis.
3. Implement precautions now: surgical mask for clinic visits, stay home from shared indoor settings, avoid close contacts, cover cough; evaluate in airborne-infection isolation room and notify infection control if TB suspected; do not order home isolation release without ID/pulmonary guidance.
4. Refer urgently: pulmonology within days for evaluation and bronchoscopy with BAL (AFB smear, MTB NAAT, mycobacterial/bacterial/fungal cultures, cytology) if sputum nondiagnostic; infectious disease urgently within days; oncology promptly to hold checkpoint immunotherapy pending workup - do not start empiric antibiotics, antifungals, or anthelminthics.
5. Conditional plan: if MTB NAAT/culture positive, place in airborne isolation, notify public health, start ID-directed multidrug therapy (do not use steroids alone) and evaluate contacts; if NTM/bacterial pathogen identified, treat per ID/pulmonary; only if infection including mycobacteria is thoroughly excluded and multidisciplinary team confirms pneumonitis should steroids be reconsidered, then with PJP prophylaxis and glucose/bone risk planning.
6. Counsel she is immunocompromised from metastatic cancer plus months of steroids, living alone needs daily check-in and plan for escalation; seek urgent/ED care for worsening dyspnea, hypoxia <92%, hemoptysis, fever, chest pain, night sweats/weight loss, or inability to complete workup; arrange PCP follow-up in 2-3 days to review results and adherence to precautions.

Grade 3 multisystem nivolumab infusion reaction at cycle 3 with cardiovascular, cutaneous and GI involvement, concerning for severe hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis with high risk of fatal recurrence on rechallenge.

1. Hold nivolumab and cancel the scheduled dose in <2 weeks in a routine outpatient infusion center; default per nivolumab labeling for Grade 3 infusion-related reaction is permanent discontinuation.
2. Refer urgently to allergy/immunology within 1 week and to medical oncology within 1 week for joint risk-benefit assessment, documentation, and evaluation for desensitization eligibility; do not rechallenge before both evaluations.
3. Evaluate now for resolution and sequelae: vitals with orthostatics, pulse oximetry, skin, cardiopulmonary and hydration exam, plus ECG, high-sensitivity troponin I, CBC, and basic metabolic panel for vomiting/diarrhea/dehydration and cardiac instability; obtain baseline serum tryptase now for future comparison.
4. Document full reaction details — timing within infusion, infusion rate/duration, premedications, lot number, concomitant dabrafenib/trametinib and anti-seizure therapy, prior cycle tolerance — in oncology and allergy records and file institutional adverse drug event and FDA MedWatch report.
5. Do not attempt routine rechallenge using premedication alone with diphenhydramine, corticosteroids, or acetaminophen, and do not switch to pembrolizumab or another PD-1 inhibitor in clinic without allergy supervision due to class cross-reactivity and risk of fatal anaphylaxis.
6. If oncology and allergy agree immunotherapy is essential, no acceptable alternative exists, and informed consent for life-threatening risk is documented, allow re-exposure only in an inpatient or ICU-capable infusion unit with a 12- to 16-step rapid desensitization protocol, continuous telemetry, pulse oximetry and blood pressure monitoring, IV access, immediately available epinephrine, oxygen, IV fluids, and prolonged observation ≥4-6 hours; draw acute serum tryptase 30-120 minutes after onset of any breakthrough symptoms.
7. Continue current dabrafenib/trametinib and anti-seizure therapy without interruption pending oncology review; review medication list for other new triggers but do not start systemic corticosteroids or antihistamines now that symptoms have resolved.
8. Counsel that rechallenge even with desensitization can cause anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest and death, that corticosteroid premedication may blunt immunotherapy efficacy and mask warning symptoms, and that stopping PD-1 therapy may affect melanoma control — confirm goals of care with patient/family and provide epinephrine autoinjector 0.3 mg IM training pending allergy visit.
9. Return precautions: call 911/go to ED immediately for dyspnea, wheeze, chest pain, palpitations, dizziness/syncope, facial/lip/tongue swelling, diffuse rash, vomiting, diarrhea, fever with shaking chills, or cyanosis; seek urgent oncology care for persistent rash, diarrhea, dyspnea, chest pain, or fatigue suggesting delayed immune toxicity.

Chronic pruritic wheals for 6 weeks resolving within 24 hours without systemic features is consistent with chronic spontaneous urticaria, not acute allergy, with inadequate control on intermittent antihistamines.

1. Start strict daily prophylaxis: cetirizine 10 mg PO once daily in evening, taken every day even when clear, continue at least 3 months after control before attempting taper. If sedation, switch to fexofenadine 180 mg PO daily or loratadine 10 mg PO daily.
2. Stop scheduled diphenhydramine: reserve only as rare rescue due to daytime sedation, impaired driving/work performance, cognitive effects, dry mouth, urinary retention, and additive sedation with alcohol. Do not drive if sedated.
3. Avoid common cofactors/worseners: NSAIDs including ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin — use acetaminophen if analgesic needed; alcohol excess; heat, vigorous rubbing/scratching, tight clothing/pressure/friction; sleep deprivation and stress; note relation to exercise, pressure, cold, vibration, infections, and new drugs. No need to change detergents further or restrict foods without history.
4. Counsel and self-monitor: individual hives should itch, blanch, migrate and fade <24 hours without bruise; disease often lasts months to years then remits, antihistamines control symptoms but do not cure, not contagious and usually not due to specific allergy. Keep brief diary with photos: duration of single lesions, pain vs itch, residual bruise/brown mark, angioedema, NSAID/alcohol/illness, response to drug.
5. No routine labs, allergy panels, total IgE, autoimmune workup, or biopsy now given classic history and no red flags; do not order food-specific IgE/skin-prick testing.
6. Escalate stepwise if not controlled after 2-4 weeks adherent daily standard dose: increase cetirizine to 10 mg BID, then up to 20 mg BID maximum (4x standard) as tolerated. Do not start chronic oral steroids, H2-blockers, leukotriene antagonists, or cyclosporine in primary care.
7. Refer to allergy/immunology or dermatology in 4-8 weeks if uncontrolled despite high-dose second-generation antihistamine for consideration of omalizumab 300 mg SC every 4 weeks; refer promptly within 1 week for possible urticarial vasculitis if individual lesions persist >24 hours, are painful/burning rather than itchy, leave purpura/bruise/hyperpigmentation, or with fever, arthralgia, abdominal pain, hematuria, elevated ESR/CRP, or poor antihistamine response — will need lesional biopsy and CBC, ESR/CRP, C3/C4, urinalysis.
8. Return precautions: seek urgent care for lip/tongue/throat swelling, dyspnea, wheeze, dysphagia, voice change, dizziness/syncope, or painful persistent hives with bruising, fever, or joint swelling.

Probable trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole hypersensitivity with acute urticaria plus concurrent AKI most consistent with immune-mediated acute interstitial nephritis as part of the drug reaction, not benign trimethoprim-related creatinine secretion inhibition, high-risk in IgA nephropathy/CKD.

1. Document TMP-SMX allergy as hives/pruritus + AKI with probable interstitial nephritis, with strict lifelong avoidance of TMP-SMX and other systemic sulfonamide antibiotics; update EHR, pharmacy and allergy list, and counsel never to retake or do home rechallenge — prior tolerance 10 years ago does not exclude new sensitization.
2. Do not order sulfa skin-prick, serum IgE, or routine patch testing; there is no validated allergy test for TMP-SMX and diagnosis is clinical. Refer to allergy/immunology routinely in 4-6 weeks for history confirmation, cross-reactivity counseling, and only to discuss desensitization if a future life-threatening indication with no alternative arises.
3. Refer to nephrology within 1-2 weeks for AKI recovery assessment on baseline Cr 1.2/IgA nephropathy with persistent trace edema; do not pursue kidney biopsy now since creatinine resolved, unless creatinine remains above baseline, proteinuria/hematuria worsens, or oliguria recurs.
4. Obtain now: basic metabolic panel with eGFR and potassium, CBC with differential for eosinophils, urinalysis with microscopy, spot urine protein/creatinine ratio, blood pressure and weight; add LFTs if rash persists, fever, lymphadenopathy, facial swelling or eosinophilia to exclude DRESS. Do not attribute Cr 2.5 to trimethoprim tubular secretion blockade alone.
5. For future UTIs base therapy on urine culture with susceptibilities and avoid empiric TMP-SMX, dapsone, sulfasalazine, sulfadiazine; non-antibiotic sulfonamides like furosemide, thiazides, celecoxib are not automatically contraindicated but use with caution and stop/report rash, swelling, fever, or decreased urine.
6. Protect kidneys especially with diabetes insipidus and CKD: maintain adequate hydration, avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxins when possible, monitor BP, and if ongoing hives/itch use cetirizine 10 mg daily as needed rather than systemic steroids or epinephrine without anaphylaxis.
7. Return precautions: seek urgent care for lip/tongue/face swelling, wheeze, dyspnea, blistering or extensive rash, fever, markedly decreased or dark/bloody urine, or worsening edema/shortness of breath.

Exertional left chest pain with dyspnea in a 50-year-old man with prediabetes, hyperlipidemia and early familial CAD is concerning for stable angina; a low 10-year ASCVD score and a negative functional stress test do not exclude obstructive CAD, and 1st-degree AV block is likely incidental.

1. Refer to cardiology in 2-4 weeks for suspected stable angina; advise no strenuous exertion until cleared and do not reassure based on ASCVD 1.2% or negative stress test alone.
2. Order coronary CT angiography with coronary artery calcium scoring as the next anatomic test for cardiac chest pain without known CAD; do not repeat functional stress testing or proceed directly to invasive coronary angiography now.
3. Retrieve prior stress test details — modality, workload/METs, % maximal predicted heart rate achieved, BP/heart-rate response, ECG and imaging findings, reason for termination, and whether typical symptoms occurred — plus repeat vitals with orthostatics, cardiac exam for murmur and heart failure signs, and resting 12-lead ECG for PR interval, QRS duration, and rate.
4. Obtain fasting lipid panel and hemoglobin A1c if not recent for risk stratification; review medications that prolong AV conduction (beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone) and obtain basic metabolic panel including potassium, calcium, magnesium. Isolated asymptomatic 1st-degree AV block needs no pacemaker, Holter, or electrophysiology referral — routine ECG follow-up only.
5. Do not start aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulation, or empiric beta-blocker/calcium-channel blocker/ranolazine pending CCTA/cardiology; continue current statin if prescribed, otherwise defer new statin initiation until lipids and CCTA are reviewed. If CCTA shows left main ≥50%, other vessel ≥70%, or high-risk anatomy, expedite to urgent cardiology for invasive angiography; if non-obstructive, optimize prevention; if normal, evaluate non-cardiac causes.
6. Return precautions: seek ED care for pain at rest, pain lasting >10 minutes despite rest, increasing frequency/severity, new dyspnea at rest, syncope/presyncope, palpitations, or hemodynamic symptoms.

Daily palpitations with fatigue in a 67-year-old man currently in sinus rhythm with only a remote 75-second AF episode and hypothyroidism suggests possible AF recurrence versus thyroid over-replacement. Stroke risk appears borderline (CHA2DS2-VA ~1) with no indication for empiric anticoagulation without documented AF burden.

1. Do NOT start a DOAC (or aspirin for AF) now in anticipation of possible ablation — bleeding risk outweighs benefit without documented recurrent clinical AF and formal stroke-risk indication, and ablation requires EP-directed uninterrupted anticoagulation for ≥3 weeks pre-procedure or TEE-guided approach, not empiric early initiation.
2. Obtain 12-lead ECG today, repeat orthostatic vitals with bilateral BP, heart rate, weight, and exam for heart failure, thyroid signs, and murmurs; review all meds/supplements, levothyroxine dose/adherence and recent changes, caffeine, decongestants, stimulants, sleep apnea symptoms, and prior hypertension, diabetes, heart failure, vascular disease, stroke/TIA, and bleeding history.
3. Order 14-day continuous ambulatory ECG monitor (e.g., Zio patch) to correlate daily palpitations with rhythm; instruct to log symptom timing, triggers, duration, and associated chest pain, dyspnea, lightheadedness, or syncope.
4. Check TSH with reflex to free T4, basic metabolic panel with magnesium and creatinine/eGFR, and CBC; do not start rate-control or antiarrhythmic while in sinus rhythm and stable.
5. Order transthoracic echocardiogram to assess left atrial size, LV function, and valvular disease given suspected recurrent AF.
6. Complete CHA2DS2-VA and HAS-BLED stratification with cardiology: if monitor confirms clinical AF, cardiology to decide on long-term DOAC via shared decision-making (typically recommended if CHA2DS2-VA ≥2; may consider if =1) and EP referral only if symptomatic AF documented — e.g., apixaban 5 mg BID (2.5 mg BID if ≥2 of age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, creatinine ≥1.5) or rivaroxaban 20 mg daily with dinner (15 mg if CrCl 15-50), without bridging.
7. Counsel that the single brief episode last year alone does not mandate lifelong anticoagulation or ablation, to avoid excess alcohol/caffeine/stimulants/NSAIDs, and to maintain routine cardiology follow-up with primary care review in 2-4 weeks for monitor, labs, and echo; seek urgent care for sustained rapid/irregular palpitations, syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, or BE-FAST stroke symptoms.

Single self-limited palpitations/tachycardia episode with paresthesias in a young man with normal exam, likely precipitated by sleep deprivation/stress/hyperventilation, plus severe hypercholesterolemia with LDL 200 concerning for familial hypercholesterolemia.

1. Retrieve ED records including presenting vitals, ED 12-lead ECG, rhythm strip, troponin timing, electrolytes, and discharge diagnosis.
2. Take focused history: palpitation frequency/duration/triggers, chest pain, dyspnea, syncope/presyncope, exertional symptoms, caffeine/energy drinks/alcohol/tobacco/cannabis/stimulants/decongestants/supplements/prescription QT-prolonging drugs, sleep pattern, anxiety/panic/hyperventilation symptoms, exertion, and family history of premature CAD <55y men/<65y women, hypercholesterolemia, sudden death, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia; check office vitals with HR/BP, orthostatics, weight/BMI, cardiac and neurologic exam including tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma, arcus cornealis.
3. Obtain resting 12-lead ECG now to compare to ED ECG; do not repeat troponin, stress test, or echo if asymptomatic with normal exam and normal ECG.
4. Obtain fasting repeat lipid panel to confirm LDL ≥190, plus baseline comprehensive metabolic panel with magnesium, CBC, and hepatic panel before statin; do not repeat TSH or A1c.
5. Start high-intensity statin for LDL ≥190: atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily long-term, or rosuvastatin 20 mg PO daily if drug-interaction concerns; counsel on muscle pain/weakness, dark urine, unexplained fatigue/jaundice, small long-term diabetes risk, and that benefit outweighs risk, with no need for routine CK monitoring unless symptoms.
6. Counsel on heart-healthy lifestyle: Mediterranean-style diet low in saturated fat/trans fat, ≥150 min/week moderate aerobic exercise, maintain healthy weight, smoking/vaping cessation if applicable, limit alcohol and avoid caffeine excess, stimulants, and sleep-deprivation triggers; refer to registered dietitian.
7. Address sleep/stress trigger with sleep hygiene, regular sleep-wake schedule, daylight exposure, limit screens/caffeine/alcohol late day, diaphragmatic breathing for panic/hyperventilation symptoms; do not start beta-blocker, calcium-channel blocker, antiarrhythmic, aspirin, or benzodiazepine/hypnotic.
8. Arrange ambulatory 14-day patch monitor and nonurgent cardiology referral only if palpitations recur, are sustained, or ECG is abnormal, or if exertional syncope, family sudden death/cardiomyopathy, murmur, or abnormal ECG; obtain echocardiogram only if those features present.
9. Follow up in 4-12 weeks with repeat fasting lipid panel, LFTs, adherence/tolerance review, and BP check, then every 3-12 months; advise first-degree relatives need lipid screening for cascade detection.
10. Return precautions: seek urgent care for chest pain/pressure, sustained palpitations >15 minutes, irregular heartbeat with dizziness/syncope, severe dyspnea, or focal weakness/numbness/speech change.

Rapid eruption of multiple seborrheic keratoses over months at age 57 is not normal aging and is concerning for Leser-Trelat sign, a possible paraneoplastic syndrome most often associated with gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma and also breast and lung cancers.

1. Refer urgently to dermatology within 1-2 weeks for clinical diagnosis with dermoscopy and punch or shave biopsy with histopathology of any atypical, ulcerated, bleeding, very dark, or rapidly changing lesions to confirm seborrheic keratosis and exclude melanoma or pigmented basal cell carcinoma; do not perform empiric wide excision, cryotherapy, or other destructive therapy in primary care.
2. See promptly in primary care for cancer-focused history and exam: B-symptoms and weight loss, dysphagia, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, bowel habit change, rectal bleeding/melena, cough, hemoptysis, change in COPD symptoms, breast lump or discharge, postmenopausal bleeding, lymphadenopathy, smoking status and pack-years, medications, family cancer history, plus complete skin, lymph node, breast, abdominal, and pelvic exam, and audit colorectal, breast, and cervical screening status.
3. Obtain CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and fecal immunochemical test (FIT); update bilateral screening mammography and cervical screening with high-risk HPV testing if overdue, and arrange colonoscopy if overdue for colorectal screening, if FIT-positive, or if anemia present. Do not order broad tumor marker panels or PET-CT as initial screening.
4. If dermatology confirms eruptive seborrheic keratoses with no alternative explanation, or if red flags, anemia, FIT positivity, or exam abnormalities are present, refer to gastroenterology within 2-4 weeks for esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy consideration and to oncology/pulmonology for contrast-enhanced CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; if exam and dermatology do not support eruptive disease, complete routine age-appropriate screening only. She does not meet USPSTF 20 pack-year criteria for lung cancer screening with low-dose CT based on 10 pack-years alone.
5. Counsel that seborrheic keratoses themselves are benign, non-contagious, and need no removal unless irritated, to avoid picking/scratching, to use gentle skin care, and explain why internal malignancy must be ruled out; ascertain current smoking, advise complete cessation, offer behavioral support plus pharmacotherapy if smoking, and ensure COPD care is current including inhaler review and influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, and RSV vaccination.
6. Reassess in 2-4 weeks to review pathology, labs, and screening completion with close surveillance over 3-6 months if initial workup is negative. Return sooner for unintentional weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting blood, black stools, rectal bleeding, persistent cough or hemoptysis, breast lump, enlarging lymph nodes, or ulceration, rapid growth, bleeding, or color change in a skin lesion.

Facial post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation following resolved allergic contact dermatitis; management is topical with strict photoprotection, with pregnancy safety and avoidance of IIH-worsening drugs as key constraints.

1. Confirm PIH clinically: document distribution, Fitzpatrick type, and ensure contact rash is inactive with no scale, vesicles or itch; review cosmetics, fragrances, hair products and topical exposures to identify and permanently avoid the contact allergen, and continue acetazolamide for IIH without interruption.
2. Obtain urine hCG now before depigmenting therapy, ask about pregnancy plans and breastfeeding, and counsel to use effective contraception while using tretinoin or hydroquinone due to teratogenicity / high systemic absorption concerns.
3. Prescribe strict daily photoprotection, critical for PIH resolution especially on acetazolamide with photosensitivity risk: broad-spectrum SPF 50+ PA++++ each morning to face, reapply every 2 hours outdoors, plus wide-brim hat, shade-seeking, and gentle skin care with mild cleanser, bland moisturizer, no picking, scrubs, home peels, prolonged topical steroids, or unregulated mercury-containing lighteners.
4. If not pregnant, not breastfeeding, and no pregnancy planned: apply triple-combination fluocinolone 0.01%/hydroquinone 4%/tretinoin 0.05% thin layer to hyperpigmented areas nightly for 8 weeks, maximum 12 weeks, with morning moisturizer and sunscreen; if irritation, reduce to every other night and add moisturizer first. Limit hydroquinone to 3 months continuous then stop for at least 3 months to avoid exogenous ochronosis. Alternative is hydroquinone 4% BID plus tretinoin 0.025% pea-sized amount nightly, same limits.
5. If pregnant, planning pregnancy, breastfeeding, or intolerant to hydroquinone/retinoid: use azelaic acid 15% gel thin layer BID to affected areas for at least 12 weeks, may continue long-term, with expectation of slower response but safe in pregnancy.
6. Do NOT use oral isotretinoin, systemic vitamin A, tetracyclines/minocycline/doxycycline which can worsen IIH, systemic corticosteroids, or oral tranexamic acid first-line for PIH; do not order biopsy, fungal, toxoplasma or IIH workup for isolated PIH.
7. Refer routinely to dermatology in 6-12 weeks if diagnosis uncertain, for patch testing to identify contact allergen if recurrent, or if no improvement after 12 weeks adherent use with photoprotection for consideration of supervised peels/laser with caution for worsening PIH; follow up in primary care in 8-12 weeks to assess response and irritation.
8. Return sooner for severe burning, blistering, spreading redness/itch suggesting active dermatitis or irritant reaction, paradoxical darkening, or signs of IIH worsening such as severe headache or vision change. Counsel PIH typically fades over 3-12 months with adherence and sun protection and recurs with UV or inflammation.

Classic capecitabine-induced palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (hand-foot syndrome), likely grade 2-3, with bilateral symmetric painful erythema, edema and fissuring. Onset after capecitabine and bilateral distribution argue against cellulitis or inflammatory arthritis, and systemic steroids are ineffective with high risk in this patient.

1. Do NOT start oral prednisone — no benefit for hand-foot syndrome and high risk at age 82 with HTN, CAD, CKD and active chemotherapy of hyperglycemia, fluid retention, hypertension, AKI, infection, delirium and falls.
2. Contact oncology same-day by phone for urgent review within 24 hours to temporarily hold capecitabine; do not restart, dose-reduce, or change oxaliplatin schedule without oncology. Continue pantoprazole — symptoms predated it.
3. Document severity now: vitals with temperature, pain score, effect on walking and hand grip/ADLs, extent of palmar/plantar erythema and digit edema, presence of blisters, ulcers, fissures, drainage, and unilateral vs bilateral spread.
4. Obtain CBC with differential, basic metabolic panel with creatinine/eGFR, and hepatic panel to assess cytopenia, CKD baseline and chemotherapy tolerance. Do not obtain joint X-rays, autoimmune labs, routine wound cultures, or dermatology biopsy unless atypical course.
5. Start supportive care: fragrance-free petrolatum ointment plus urea 10% cream to hands and feet BID, lukewarm washing only, cool compresses 15 min TID, elevation, loose cotton socks/gloves, cushioned loose footwear; avoid hot water, heat, friction/pressure, tight shoes, prolonged standing/walking, and manual friction.
6. Treat pain with acetaminophen 500-1000 mg q6h PRN, max 3000 mg/24h; avoid NSAIDs including celecoxib and avoid opioids as first-line given CKD, CAD, HTN and age. Do not start empiric antibiotics or topical/systemic steroids.
7. Counsel that hand-foot syndrome typically improves within 1-2 weeks of holding capecitabine, that oncology will decide on dose reduction vs resumption, and to keep fissures clean with petrolatum, avoid picking, and report increased pain, spreading redness, pus, or fever.
8. Recheck in person in 48-72 hours for pain, edema, fissures, function and signs of superinfection, with earlier oncology follow-up as directed. If blistering/ulceration, purulent drainage, fever ≥100.4F, rapidly expanding or markedly unilateral erythema, or inability to walk or use hands, seek same-day urgent care for evaluation for secondary cellulitis.

78-year-old at high fracture risk on short-course oral alendronate (1 year) without additional MRONJ risk factors who needs elective invasive dentoalveolar surgery; MRONJ risk is very low and fracture risk outweighs any benefit of interrupting antiresorptive therapy.

1. Continue alendronate without drug holiday: no preoperative hold and no delayed resumption needed. Per AAOMS, oral bisphosphonate <4 years without risk factors (corticosteroids, diabetes, smoking, rheumatoid arthritis, cancer, anti-angiogenic therapy, prior MRONJ) does not require interruption for dentoalveolar surgery. Take next weekly dose on schedule post-op as soon as she can sit upright 30-60 minutes and swallow; a 1-week delay for post-op intolerance is inconsequential, not a formal holiday.
2. Continue aspirin for TIA secondary prevention and atorvastatin perioperatively. Do not stop aspirin for single-tooth extraction with graft/implant; use local hemostatic measures and advise dentist of TIA history. Stopping increases stroke risk with minimal bleeding benefit.
3. Do not order routine serum CTX, bone turnover markers, urgent DEXA, or urgent labs to decide on MRONJ risk – they are not predictive and should not delay surgery. Optimize only what affects healing: treat active dental/periodontal infection first, ensure adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D repletion if already prescribed, reinforce oral hygiene, smoking cessation if applicable, and atraumatic technique with primary closure per oral surgeon; chlorhexidine/antibiotics per dentist protocol only.
4. Counsel with shared decision-making: MRONJ with 1-year oral alendronate for osteopenia is rare (~0.01-0.1%), but extraction + graft + implant is higher risk than simple extraction and has higher implant failure/non-integration risk on antiresorptives. Discuss alternatives – bridge, removable partial denture, or no replacement – especially given age and anxiety, and need for long-term dental surveillance. Document informed consent with dentist/oral surgeon.
5. Coordinate routine osteoporosis care with PCP, no urgent endocrinology referral needed: continue alendronate given high fracture risk, fall prevention, weight-bearing activity as tolerated, limit alcohol, adequate calcium/vitamin D, and routine DEXA/FRAX interval monitoring; reassess need for long-term therapy at 5 years, not now.
6. Return precautions and follow-up: routine dental follow-up for mucosal/osseous healing over 8-12 weeks; seek prompt oral surgery evaluation for exposed bone, socket that fails to heal >2 weeks, persistent pain, swelling, pus, bleeding, lip/chin numbness, or loosening implant concerning for MRONJ/infection. If MRONJ features develop, refer urgently to oral and maxillofacial surgery and notify prescribing physician.

Lean, catabolic older adult with worsening hyperglycemia despite therapy, 4.6% weight loss in 1 month to BMI 19.7 and fasting > postprandial glucose suggests insulin deficiency/LADA rather than typical type 2 diabetes, with active weight loss making GLP-1–induced anorexia/sarcopenia unsafe and raising concern for secondary cause including pancreatic disease.

1. Do not start dulaglutide or other injectable GLP-1 RA and do not titrate oral semaglutide — 3 mg Rybelsus is subtherapeutic yet already associated with weight loss; dulaglutide will worsen anorexia, nausea, weight/sarcopenia, frailty/fall risk and is inadequate for likely insulin deficiency.
2. Discontinue Rybelsus 3 mg daily now; do not restart pioglitazone — contraindicated with osteoporosis/fracture risk, trace edema, and heart failure risk; avoid SGLT2 inhibitor, and clarify sitagliptin does not cause osteoporosis but DPP-4 is insufficient for catabolic hyperglycemia.
3. Obtain promptly: A1c, BMP with eGFR, CMP with albumin/LFTs/calcium, CBC, TSH with reflex to free T4, vitamin B12, 25-OH vitamin D, fasting C-peptide with concurrent venous glucose, anti-GAD65 plus IA-2 and ZnT8 if available, serum beta-hydroxybutyrate, urinalysis and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio; review SMBG log, BP, meds, smoking/alcohol, GI symptoms, stool change, abdominal pain, appetite, malignancy and autoimmune/thyroid history, and verify age-appropriate cancer screening.
4. Start basal insulin for fasting hyperglycemia/catabolism: e.g., insulin glargine U-100 7-8 units subQ at bedtime (~0.15 U/kg at 47 kg), titrate by 2 units every 3-4 days to fasting 90-130 mg/dL if no hypoglycemia; if C-peptide low, antibodies positive, or ketones positive, do not delay intensification. Continue metformin 1000 mg BID only if eGFR >45, no dehydration, GI intolerance or B12 deficiency; hold during acute illness, vomiting, dehydration or contrast exposure.
5. Prescribe SMBG 4x daily (fasting and 2-hr post-meal) or preferably continuous glucose monitor (Libre/Dexcom), and counsel on hypoglycemia: 15g fast carbs, recheck in 15 min, glucagon prescription, driving and fall precautions, and titration hold if glucose <70 mg/dL.
6. Evaluate unintentional weight loss and edema: exam for lymphadenopathy, breast, thyroid, abdomen, cardiac/lung; check weight twice weekly, albumin, renal function and diet review; if no clear cause, smoking history, persistent loss, abdominal symptoms, steatorrhea or new diabetes in lean older adult, obtain contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis with pancreatic protocol — coordinate via endocrinology/primary care, do not order broad tumor markers or PET routinely.
7. Refer urgently to endocrinology within 1-2 weeks for LADA/insulin management and pancreatic workup, registered dietitian within 2-4 weeks for high-protein weight-maintenance plan plus resistance activity as tolerated, and primary care in 1 week for weight, edema, glucose review; bone health: DEXA, calcium/vitamin D repletion, osteoporosis management — avoid bone-toxic/weight-loss diabetes drugs.
8. Return precautions: seek urgent care for nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, fruity breath, polyuria/polydipsia with glucose >250 mg/dL (possible DKA even without prior type 1 diagnosis), recurrent glucose <70 mg/dL, confusion, chest pain, dyspnea, worsening edema, or continued weight loss.

Progressive iron-deficiency anemia in a 76-year-old anticoagulated man with high stroke risk and negative recent bidirectional endoscopy suggests ongoing occult small-bowel blood loss exacerbated but not caused by apixaban.

1. Continue apixaban without interruption; do not stop or switch to left atrial appendage closure now. With CHA2DS2-VASc 5 stroke risk outweighs transfusion-independent occult bleeding, and Watchman is reserved for absolute contraindication to anticoagulation or recurrent major/life-threatening bleeding despite treatable source correction.
2. Request cardiology review in 2-4 weeks to reconcile antithrombotics: confirm stent date/type and indication, and if >12 months post-stent with stable CAD and no recent ACS/PCI, discontinue concomitant aspirin/clopidogrel and continue apixaban monotherapy. Avoid NSAIDs, excess alcohol, and dual therapy; add PPI only if aspirin/NSAID must continue.
3. Obtain CBC with differential, reticulocyte count, iron panel with ferritin, vitamin B12, folate, CMP, and urinalysis with microscopy; review medication/supplement list, NSAID/iron/PPI use, diet, hematuria, epistaxis, and obtain prior EGD/colonoscopy reports to confirm adequate prep, cecal intubation, and duodenal biopsies.
4. Start iron repletion, e.g., ferrous sulfate 325 mg (65 mg elemental) PO every other day for 3 months, taken with vitamin C away from tea/coffee/antacids, with repeat hemoglobin/ferritin in 4-8 weeks; use IV iron if intolerant, malabsorption, inadequate response, or Hgb severely low/symptomatic.
5. Refer to gastroenterology in 2-4 weeks for small-bowel evaluation with video capsule endoscopy as next step given negative adequate EGD/colonoscopy within 1 year; do not attribute IDA to hemorrhoids or diverticulosis and do not repeat EGD/colonoscopy now unless prior exams were incomplete/inadequate. Continue apixaban for capsule; hold only for therapeutic enteroscopy per GI/cardiology.
6. If capsule shows angioectasia, ulcer, or mass, proceed to device-assisted enteroscopy for hemostasis/biopsy/resection; if capsule negative, monitor on iron with periodic CBC, and consider CT/MR enterography only if concern for stricture/mass or capsule retention risk.
7. Counsel to report melena, hematochezia, hematemesis, gross hematuria, syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, or palpitations, and seek urgent care for those, symptomatic anemia, or need for transfusion; routine urology referral only if gross/microscopic hematuria suggests urinary blood loss.

Persistent mild fasting hyperprolactinemia in a 40-year-old man with erectile dysfunction and no medication or renal cause. Microprolactinomas commonly present without headache or visual symptoms, so mass-effect symptoms cannot rule out adenoma and secondary causes must be excluded first.

1. Take focused history: libido, fertility desire, infertility, galactorrhea, gynecomastia, headache, vision change, chest-wall trauma/surgery, nipple stimulation, strenuous exercise, sleep deprivation, stress or venipuncture difficulty before draws, alcohol, cannabis, anabolic steroids, and review all prescription, OTC, herbal and GI/antipsychotic/antihypertensive/opioid use. Examine vitals/BMI, confrontation visual fields, breasts for discharge/gynecomastia, genitalia/testicular volume and secondary sexual characteristics.
2. Obtain TSH with reflex to free T4, comprehensive metabolic panel with creatinine/eGFR and liver tests, 8-10 AM fasting total testosterone with LH and FSH, and macroprolactin by polyethylene glycol precipitation to determine monomeric bioactive prolactin. No additional prolactin repeat now given two adequate fasting morning samples; do not order full pituitary panel, tumor markers, or routine visual fields at this stage.
3. If TSH and creatinine/liver tests are normal and monomeric prolactin remains elevated, obtain dedicated MRI sella/pituitary with and without gadolinium routinely in next 4-6 weeks — not non-contrast brain MRI or CT — to evaluate for microadenoma or stalk lesion despite prolactin only 27-30 ng/mL and no visual symptoms. If macroprolactin predominant with normal monomeric prolactin, defer MRI.
4. Do not start cabergoline, bromocriptine, or testosterone replacement empirically. Refer to outpatient endocrinology in 4-8 weeks for hyperprolactinemia management; if MRI shows macroadenoma ≥10 mm, chiasmal contact, or hypopituitarism, escalate to urgent endocrinology plus neuro-ophthalmology with formal visual fields. Avoid new dopamine antagonists such as antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, verapamil, or opioids if alternatives exist.
5. Counsel that mild hyperprolactinemia can suppress GnRH causing low libido, erectile dysfunction and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, but ED at this age is often multifactorial; reassure most microadenomas are benign and medically treatable without surgery, and advise avoiding nipple stimulation, chest irritation, strenuous exercise and sexual activity for 24 hours before any future prolactin draw.
6. Return sooner for new severe headache, vision loss, diplopia, visual field cut, galactorrhea, or gynecomastia.

Recurrent hematochezia with change in stool caliber in a 70-year-old with prior left colectomy is high-risk for colorectal neoplasia/anastomotic disease until proven otherwise; normal CT angiography only excludes active brisk bleeding and does not exclude mass, polyp, stricture, or intermittent bleeding source.

1. Obtain outside hospital records including Hgb trend, transfusions, CT angiography report/images, and medication list, plus operative and pathology reports from prior left colectomy and any prior colonoscopy/polyp history for the endoscopist.
2. Perform prompt in-office evaluation: orthostatic vitals, cardiopulmonary and abdominal exam, digital rectal and anorectal exam; detailed history of bleeding volume, frequency, clots, melena, abdominal pain, weight loss, obstructive symptoms, CRC screening/family CRC history, smoking, NSAID/alcohol/anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, and HF symptoms including dyspnea, edema, chest pain, syncope.
3. Order CBC with platelets, basic metabolic panel for renal function/prep planning, and iron studies with ferritin and transferrin saturation; obtain 12-lead ECG for LBBB baseline and review recent echocardiogram for LV function — repeat echo and involve cardiology/anesthesia only if no study in past year, worsening HF, chest pain/syncope, or concern for high sedation risk. Do not order FIT/FOBT, CEA, or repeat CT angiography.
4. Refer urgently to gastroenterology within 1-2 weeks for complete colonoscopy with notification of altered anatomy/anastomosis; do not delay or reassure based on stable vitals/Hgb or normal CTA, and do not attribute caliber change to hemorrhoids.
5. Optimize periprocedural safety: use iso-osmotic polyethylene glycol prep, avoid sodium phosphate or magnesium-based preps in elderly with LV dysfunction/diabetes/possible CKD; provide bowel-prep fasting instructions with diabetes medication, diuretic and antihypertensive adjustments; coordinate any anticoagulant/antiplatelet interruption with prescribing clinician; avoid NSAIDs.
6. Plan contingencies: if mass/stricture found, urgent colorectal surgery referral; if colonoscopy negative or incomplete, pursue GI-directed next steps such as EGD given PUD/prior GI bleed history and/or CT colonography or small-bowel evaluation rather than observation; if progressive narrowing, obstipation, vomiting or distension, send to ED for obstruction evaluation.
7. Counsel that stability does not rule out cancer, explain need for complete visualization and adequate prep, and arrange PCP follow-up within 1 week to confirm GI appointment, review labs, and recheck symptoms, vitals and Hgb.
8. Return precautions: seek emergency care for large-volume hematochezia, dizziness, syncope, palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea, severe abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, or inability to pass stool/flatus.

Asymptomatic 45-year-old with persistent FIT positivity ~1 year after complete colonoscopy with low-risk adenomas resected. Recent colonoscopy makes colorectal cancer/advanced adenoma very unlikely; results likely reflect benign anorectal source and inappropriate FIT use for diarrhea evaluation and for post-polypectomy surveillance.

1. Do not repeat colonoscopy now and do not refer to gastroenterology urgently; maintain existing surveillance interval — repeat colonoscopy in 4 years (5 years from index) unless new alarm features or anemia develop, do not shorten interval for FIT positivity.
2. Stop FIT testing; do not repeat FIT for surveillance or for diarrhea workup — FIT is for average-risk screening, not for symptomatic evaluation or post-polypectomy surveillance.
3. Verify quality of prior colonoscopy from report: cecal intubation with photo documentation, adequacy of bowel prep, complete polyp resection, and withdrawal; if inadequate or incomplete, discuss with gastroenterology, otherwise accept as clearing.
4. Take focused bleeding history: visible rectal bleeding, hemorrhoids, anal fissure/pain, epistaxis/gum bleeding, hematuria, NSAID use, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, alcohol use; do not stop indicated anticoagulant/antiplatelet, review NSAID necessity.
5. Perform focused examination including vitals and anorectal inspection plus digital rectal exam for hemorrhoids, fissure, mass or blood; if active benign anorectal source found, treat accordingly.
6. Obtain CBC to exclude anemia; check ferritin/iron studies and refer to gastroenterology promptly only if anemic or iron-deficient. Do not obtain CEA, stool culture/O&P, fecal calprotectin, EGD, CT colonography or other imaging while asymptomatic.
7. Counsel that resolved traveler's diarrhea needs no further infectious workup now, that FIT can be falsely positive from hemorrhoidal/fissure bleeding, and that future screening should be colonoscopy-based per surveillance interval, not FIT.
8. Return precautions: seek prompt care for hematochezia, melena, persistent abdominal pain, change in bowel habits, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, or dizziness; if these occur or anemia develops, expedite GI referral for colonoscopy ± upper GI evaluation.

Severe iron-deficiency anemia (Hgb 7.3 g/dL, MCV 67, ferritin <5 ng/mL) refractory to intermittent oral iron, most consistent with true iron deficiency from ongoing blood loss or malabsorption, not thalassemia trait.

1. Do not order hemoglobinopathy work-up now (no hemoglobin electrophoresis, alpha-globin testing, or Mentzer calculation). Ferritin <5 ng/mL with severe microcytic hypochromic anemia establishes iron deficiency; thalassemia trait does not cause absent stores and would not present de novo at age 52 without family history.
2. Assess acuity now: orthostatic vitals, cardiopulmonary symptoms, active bleeding (melena, hematochezia, hematemesis, hematuria, menorrhagia), NSAID/anticoagulant/antiplatelet/PPI use, diet, weight loss, bowel habit change, prior pregnancies, menstrual history, GI surgery, and adherence/dosing of oral iron. Transfuse only for hemodynamic instability, ischemic symptoms, or active major bleeding, not for Hgb 7.3 alone.
3. Treat with IV iron given severity and oral iron failure: e.g., ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg IV, repeat 750 mg 7 days later; discontinue ineffective intermittent oral iron. Recheck CBC with differential and reticulocyte count and ferritin in 4-8 weeks; failure to rise Hgb by ~1-2 g/dL should prompt hematology referral.
4. Obtain: repeat CBC with differential, reticulocyte count, fecal immunochemical test (FIT), urinalysis with microscopy and urine culture, and tissue transglutaminase IgA with quantitative total IgA for celiac screen. Review peripheral smear already done; no additional tumor markers, CT, or marrow biopsy.
5. Refer urgently to gastroenterology within 2 weeks for bidirectional endoscopy (EGD and colonoscopy) for new severe IDA at age 52 to exclude GI blood loss/malignancy, even without GI symptoms. If bidirectional endoscopy negative and anemia persists/recurs, proceed to small-bowel evaluation with video capsule endoscopy and H. pylori stool antigen testing.
6. Refer to gynecology within 2-4 weeks for abnormal uterine bleeding evaluation (menstrual quantification, pelvic exam, pelvic ultrasound if bleeding history). Stop chronic intermittent phenazopyridine (Pyridium); evaluate recurrent urinary symptoms for UTI vs hematuria as blood-loss source and counsel that it causes orange urine, interferes with dipstick UA, and risks methemoglobinemia, hemolysis, and renal injury with prolonged use.
7. Return precautions: seek urgent care for syncope, chest pain, dyspnea at rest, palpitations, hematemesis, melena, large-volume hematochezia, heavy vaginal bleeding soaking >1 pad/hour, or gross hematuria with clots.

Stable isolated mild thrombocytopenia at 100-150k for 3 years in an otherwise healthy young woman is most consistent with chronic primary ITP or benign stable thrombocytopenia, with low bleeding risk and no features of marrow failure, malignancy, liver disease or hypersplenism.

1. Confirm true thrombocytopenia: repeat CBC with differential and have peripheral blood smear reviewed for platelet clumping, platelet size/morphology, blasts, dysplasia, schistocytes, and WBC/RBC abnormalities; repeat platelet count in sodium citrate tube to exclude EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia.
2. Review prior records including pre-pregnancy, pregnancy, and peripartum platelet counts and cause of postpartum hemorrhage, plus focused bleeding history, autoimmune symptoms, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, infections, alcohol use, diet, and complete medication/supplement review for thrombocytopenia-associated drugs.
3. Obtain HIV-1/2 Ag/Ab combo and hepatitis C antibody with reflex to HCV RNA as secondary causes of ITP; do not order broad autoimmune panels, H. pylori testing, B12/folate/iron, abdominal imaging, inherited platelet disorder genetics, or bone marrow biopsy in stable isolated mild thrombocytopenia without other cytopenias, blasts, dysplasia, or systemic signs.
4. Do not start corticosteroids, IVIG, anti-D, TPO-receptor agonists, immunosuppressants, or platelet transfusion for asymptomatic platelets ~110k without bleeding, pregnancy, or imminent surgery.
5. Refer routinely to hematology in 4-12 weeks for diagnostic confirmation and longitudinal plan; no urgent/emergent referral needed.
6. Monitor with CBC with differential every 6-12 months if stable, and recheck promptly before invasive procedures, dental surgery, delivery, or neuraxial anesthesia, and once per trimester if pregnant; coordinate periprocedural/obstetric plan with hematology and obstetrics.
7. Counsel that counts >100k carry minimal spontaneous bleeding risk and require no activity restriction, but advise to report prolonged bleeding, to inform proceduralists/obstetrician of thrombocytopenia history, to avoid NSAIDs when possible, excess alcohol, and new platelet-lowering drugs, and that future pregnancy needs platelet monitoring for maternal bleeding and small risk of neonatal thrombocytopenia if ITP.
8. Expedite hematology evaluation if platelets fall persistently <50k and urgently if <30k, active mucosal bleeding, new anemia/leukopenia/neutropenia, fever, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or need for urgent surgery/delivery.
9. Return precautions: seek prompt care for petechiae/purpura, epistaxis or gum bleeding >10 minutes, menorrhagia, hematuria, melena, hemoptysis, severe headache/neurologic change, or bleeding after trauma/procedure.

Latent TB infection in an asymptomatic adult from an endemic country with positive QFT and normal chest X-ray. No features of active TB, so urgent multidrug TB treatment is not indicated and short-term deferral is safe after rapid HIV/risk assessment.

1. Confirm no active TB now and document: review TB symptoms (cough >2-3 weeks, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis), TB history/treatment, BCG, exposures, occupation risks, alcohol use, liver disease, and medications/immunosuppression; review exam and PA chest X-ray. No sputum AFB smear/culture/NAAT, chest CT, repeat QFT, or isolation/work restriction/contact investigation needed without symptoms or X-ray abnormality.
2. Assess reactivation risk promptly, do not delay this: obtain HIV-1/2 4th-generation Ag/Ab, HbA1c for diabetes screening, and focused review for HIV risk, diabetes, CKD, silicosis, gastrectomy, smoking, TNF-inhibitor/steroid use, and transplant/cancer chemotherapy. If HIV-positive, recently exposed, or otherwise immunocompromised, do not defer — refer urgently to infectious disease/TB clinic.
3. Deferral for a few months is acceptable if assessment in #2 is negative: document shared decision, schedule primary care follow-up in 2-3 months to re-screen symptoms and initiate treatment, with interval chest X-ray only if symptoms develop. No routine pulmonary/ID referral needed; consider local health department TB program for treatment support when ready.
4. When ready, treat LTBI with a short-course rifamycin regimen after re-confirming no active TB symptoms and reviewing drug interactions (warfarin, statins, antiepileptics, antiretrovirals, methadone): e.g., rifampin 10 mg/kg up to 600 mg PO daily for 4 months (120 doses) OR 12 weekly doses of isoniazid 15 mg/kg up to 900 mg + rifapentine 900 mg if ≥50 kg (750 mg if 32-49.9 kg) + pyridoxine 25-50 mg weekly. Avoid 6-9 months isoniazid alone unless rifamycin contraindicated. Obtain baseline AST/ALT and total bilirubin at treatment start (plus hepatitis B surface Ag/Ab/core Ab and hepatitis C Ab given endemic origin/liver risk), counsel to avoid alcohol, and monitor monthly for hepatitis/rash.
5. Counsel: LTBI is not contagious, does not require isolation, but carries ~5-10% lifetime reactivation risk; treatment reduces risk by >90%. Rifamycins cause orange urine/tears, GI upset, hepatotoxicity, and reduce effectiveness of many drugs.
6. Return sooner for cough >2-3 weeks, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis, jaundice, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, or rash — hold LTBI treatment plan and obtain repeat chest X-ray and urgent TB evaluation with sputum NAAT/culture if active TB suspected.

Remote single isolated subsegmental PE treated with 3 months apixaban 3.5 years ago with no recurrence is a low-risk phenotype where surveillance is favored over indefinite anticoagulation, with net harm from restarting now given bleeding and drug-interaction risks in a kidney-transplant recipient.

1. Do not resume apixaban or other indefinite anticoagulation; continue off anticoagulation with clinical surveillance.
2. Retrieve index CT pulmonary angiography report/images and records of bilateral proximal lower-extremity compression duplex ultrasound at diagnosis, periprocedural immobilization, hospitalization, hormones, smoking, and COVID to confirm truly isolated unprovoked subsegmental event; document bleeding-risk review including CBC with platelets, basic metabolic panel with creatinine/eGFR, blood pressure, concurrent antiplatelet/NSAID use, alcohol, fall risk, and transplant immunosuppressants with levels.
3. Do not obtain routine repeat CT angiography, D-dimer, surveillance leg duplex, inherited/acquired thrombophilia panel, or expanded malignancy workup while asymptomatic; no urgent hematology referral needed — continue age-appropriate cancer screening and routine transplant nephrology follow-up.
4. Evaluate ferritin 1059 ng/mL in limited fashion: obtain fasting serum iron, TIBC with calculated transferrin saturation, C-reactive protein, AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin, and review IV/oral iron, transfusions, alcohol and liver history; do not start iron, phlebotomy or chelation — if transferrin saturation >45%, LFTs abnormal, or persistent rise, refer nonurgently to transplant nephrology/hepatology.
5. Counsel with shared decision-making why indefinite anticoagulation is not indicated, bleeding risks and DOAC interactions with cyclosporine/tacrolimus, and VTE mitigation: early mobilization after illness/surgery, avoid prolonged immobility/dehydration, and plan procedure-, hospitalization- or long-travel-related prophylaxis with transplant team.
6. If new confirmed proximal DVT or PE occurs, start therapeutic anticoagulation promptly with transplant nephrology/pharmacy co-management for graft function and interactions; seek urgent care for unilateral leg swelling/pain, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, or bleeding.

Receptive vaginal exposure to a partner with likely viremia (recent HIV diagnosis), presenting >72 hours post-exposure. Efficacy of non-occupational PEP is limited to ≤72 hours, so PEP is not indicated for this exposure and baseline risk is HIV/STI acquisition and pregnancy.

1. Do NOT prescribe HIV nPEP for exposure >72 hours ago – no demonstrated benefit, with risk of toxicity, drug interactions, and false reassurance. Explain rationale and document shared decision-making.
2. Clarify exposure timeline in detail: date/time of last and all exposures in past 2 weeks, type of sex, condom use, partner’s HIV viral load, ART use/adherence, STI history, patient’s prior HIV tests, HBV vaccination, contraception, LMP, and ongoing sexual contact. If a separate exposure occurred within 72 hours, start 28-day nPEP immediately per CDC (e.g., tenofovir disoproxil 300mg/emtricitabine 200mg daily + dolutegravir 50mg daily or raltegravir 400mg BID) and refer urgently to ID/ED.
3. Obtain baseline 4th-generation HIV-1/2 p24 antigen/antibody immunoassay now to establish pre-exposure status; do not order routine HIV RNA unless acute retroviral symptoms present.
4. Screen for co-transmitted infections: syphilis treponemal test with reflex RPR, vaginal NAAT for gonorrhea/chlamydia (add pharyngeal/rectal NAAT if exposed sites), HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc, and hepatitis C antibody with reflex HCV RNA.
5. Assess pregnancy risk: urine hCG now plus LMP and contraception history. If exposure within 120 hours/5 days, offer emergency contraception – ulipristal acetate 30mg PO single dose (preferred if >72h) or copper IUD placement within 5 days; levonorgestrel is ineffective >72h.
6. Counsel on risk reduction: condoms for all sex until follow-up complete, partner linkage to HIV care and sustained viral suppression (U=U), no work restriction for teaching, and no blood/tissue donation during window.
7. Evaluate for HIV PrEP given ongoing risk with serodifferent partner not known to be suppressed: discuss daily tenofovir-based PrEP or long-acting cabotegravir/lenacapavir. If interested, check serum creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis, pregnancy test, and HBV panel already drawn, and refer to sexual health/PrEP clinic or ID within 1-2 weeks; offer HBV vaccination if non-immune.
8. Arrange follow-up: repeat 4th-generation HIV test at 6 weeks and 12 weeks post-exposure, review STI results in 1 week and treat if positive, and retest STIs at 2 weeks if high concern.
9. Return precautions: seek prompt care for fever, rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, myalgia/arthralgia, headache, or vomiting/diarrhea within 2-4 weeks for acute HIV evaluation with HIV RNA testing.

Post-azithromycin persistent loose but non-watery stools without fever, abdominal pain, or frequent diarrhea in a patient with prior recurrent C. difficile s/p fecal transplant most likely reflects antibiotic-associated upset rather than active C. difficile, and testing now without meeting clinical thresholds risks false-positive detection of colonization.

1. Do not order C. difficile testing at this time; history of fecal transplant and recent azithromycin alone are not indications, and do not submit formed or merely loose but non-diarrheal stool.
2. Quantify bowel pattern over next 48-72 hours: number of unformed stools per 24 hours, Bristol type, laxative, stool softener, magnesium, new diet/supplement use, and pneumonia course; azithromycin-related loose stools typically resolve within a few days of completion.
3. Do not start empiric C. difficile therapy with oral vancomycin, fidaxomicin, or metronidazole, and avoid loperamide or diphenoxylate-atropine while bloody stool history and possible C. difficile risk remain unresolved; maintain oral hydration.
4. Practice antibiotic stewardship: complete azithromycin only if still indicated for the atypical pneumonia, then stop; avoid new systemic antibiotics, and do not start or continue proton-pump inhibitor unless clearly indicated.
5. If she develops new-onset ≥3 unformed watery stools (Bristol 6-7) in 24 hours off laxatives, especially with crampy abdominal pain, fever, leukocytosis, or recurrent bloody stools, then submit a single unformed stool for C. difficile GDH antigen plus toxin A/B EIA with reflex to NAAT for tcdB; do not order test-of-cure after treatment.
6. Follow up with primary care in 3-5 days or sooner if worsening; no urgent GI or ID referral now — contact GI who performed transplant promptly if testing becomes positive or bloody diarrhea recurs for evaluation of recurrence vs inflammatory bowel disease/ischemic colitis.
7. Return precautions: seek sooner care for ≥3 watery stools/day, fever, worsening abdominal pain/cramping, vomiting, dizziness/dehydration, or any recurrence of bloody stools.

Mild creatinine elevation with normal cystatin C, bland urinalyses, normotension and no nephrotoxins suggests creatinine overestimation from muscle mass, diet, exercise or supplements rather than true CKD; the 1.2 to 1.4 change needs confirmation of true GFR and current albuminuria.

1. Confirm true GFR with same-day basic metabolic panel with CKD-EPI 2021 eGFRcreatinine plus cystatin C with eGFRcystatin and eGFRcreatinine-cystatin, plus BUN, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphorus, albumin; repeat in 2-4 weeks euvolemic, same lab, avoiding heavy resistance exercise, large meat meal, dehydration, NSAIDs and creatine for 24-48 hours before draw.
2. Update proteinuria/hematuria assessment now – first-morning spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and urinalysis with microscopy; if UACR 30-300 mg/g repeat twice over 3 months to confirm persistence, if UACR >300 mg/g or active sediment with dysmorphic RBCs/RBC casts/proteinuria proceed to nephrology workup.
3. Focused review: BMI/muscle mass, resistance training, protein intake, creatine/whey, anabolic steroids, NSAIDs, diuretics, volume depletion, recent illness, family history of CKD/ESKD, stones, hearing loss, hypertension/diabetes; exam for edema, orthostatics, and 7-day home BP log; check hemoglobin A1c with fasting glucose and CBC once.
4. Defer repeat kidney ultrasound, extensive serologies (ANA, ANCA, complements, hepatitis/HIV, SPEP), CT, and biopsy given normal ultrasound 5 years ago, bland UA, normal BP and normal cystatin C; obtain repeat renal ultrasound for size/echogenicity/obstruction only if combined eGFR <60, persistent UACR ≥30, persistent hematuria, anemia, hyperkalemia, or acidosis.
5. Counsel that normal cystatin C makes true GFR impairment unlikely and CKD requires persistent eGFR <60 or albuminuria >3 months; advise maintain euhydration, avoid NSAIDs and creatine/anabolic supplements if used, limit sodium to ~2g/day, maintain healthy weight, continue no smoking.
6. Follow-up in primary care in 3-6 months with repeat creatinine/cystatin C, UACR, and BP; refer routinely to nephrology (non-urgent, 3-6 months) only if eGFRcr-cys <60, persistent UACR ≥30, creatinine rise >30% on repeat, or CKD complications develop; seek prompt care for oliguria, gross hematuria, foamy urine, new edema, flank pain, vomiting, or BP >160/100.

Incidental renal infarct with preserved blood pressure and renal function in a 60-year-old with ovarian cancer history most likely represents cardioembolic, aortic/renal atherosclerotic, or malignancy-associated arterial thrombosis; priority is determining acuity and embolic source for secondary prevention rather than emergent revascularization.

1. Clarify acuity and context: onset/duration of flank/abdominal pain, hematuria, fever, oliguria, palpitations, syncope, stroke/TIA, claudication, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, known atrial fibrillation, valvular disease, endocarditis risk, recent arterial/venous clot, catheter/procedure, bleeding history, ovarian cancer status (active vs remission), recent chemotherapy especially anti-VEGF/bevacizumab, hormonal therapy, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use; exam with bilateral arm BP, heart rate/rhythm and murmur, carotid/renal bruits, peripheral pulses, edema, skin embolic lesions, neurologic exam.
2. Formally over-read surveillance CT with abdominal radiologist and obtain CTA abdomen/pelvis with arterial phase to characterize infarct age/size, renal artery thrombus/stenosis/dissection, aortic atheroma/thrombus, and concurrent splenic, mesenteric, or venous thromboembolism; do not proceed to catheter angiography or intervention given normotension and normal creatinine without acute abdomen/AKI.
3. Complete cardioembolic workup: 12-lead ECG, transthoracic echocardiogram to assess LV thrombus, valvular vegetations including marantic endocarditis, ejection fraction and shunt, and 14-day ambulatory ECG patch monitor for occult atrial fibrillation; obtain blood cultures and urgent TEE/cardiology input only if fever, murmur, bacteremia, multiple systemic infarcts, or valvular lesion on TTE.
4. Obtain CBC, basic metabolic panel with eGFR, urinalysis with microscopy, spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, LDH, ESR and CRP, fasting lipid panel, and hemoglobin A1c; review oncology records for cancer activity, CA-125 trend, and recent imaging; do not order routine inherited thrombophilia panel, lupus anticoagulant/anticardiolipin/beta2-glycoprotein, ANCA/ANA, or renal biopsy without recurrent thrombosis, systemic vasculitis features, or obstetric/autoimmune clues.
5. Defer empiric anticoagulation or thrombolysis; if embolic atrial fibrillation or intracardiac/aortic thrombus is confirmed, anticoagulate per cardiology/oncology balancing bleeding and cancer-related risk, and if atherosclerotic renal/aortic disease without embolus, manage with antiplatelet and high-intensity statin per cardiology/nephrology — do not start dual therapy or heparin bridge in primary care alone.
6. Institute home BP monitoring and repeat basic metabolic panel with eGFR and urinalysis in 1-2 weeks, then q1-3 months for 6 months to detect renovascular hypertension, proteinuria, or CKD progression; reinforce smoking cessation, diabetes/lipid control, hydration, and avoidance of NSAIDs/aminoglycosides/iodinated contrast without indication.
7. Refer to cardiology within 2 weeks for rhythm/echo interpretation and antithrombotic decision, nephrology in 2-4 weeks for renal prognosis and BP/proteinuria management, and oncology promptly to confirm cancer status and thrombosis risk; send to ED emergently only for acute severe flank pain, AKI, anuria, malignant hypertension, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations with syncope, or focal neurologic deficit.
8. Counsel that small unilateral infarcts often remain asymptomatic with stable function but carry recurrent stroke/MI/renal infarct risk until source treated; seek sooner care for new flank pain, visible hematuria, decreased urine, BP >180/110 mmHg, chest pain, irregular pulse, dyspnea, leg swelling/pain, or stroke symptoms.

Dilute polyuria with nocturia persisting after UTI therapy and normal glucose, kidney function and calcium suggests hypotonic polyuria — central vs nephrogenic diabetes insipidus vs primary polydipsia — rather than bacterial cystitis.

1. Confirm true polyuria with 3-day frequency-volume diary including timed fluid intake, urine volumes, caffeine/alcohol, and nocturia episodes, plus 24-hour urine collection for total volume, creatinine for completeness, osmolality, sodium, and glucose; polyuria is >3 L/day.
2. Obtain paired morning serum osmolality and serum sodium with urine osmolality, urine sodium, and urine glucose; rely on recent normal CMP and A1c and do not repeat them, repeat ankle imaging, or start empiric antibiotics. Review medications specifically for lithium, diuretics, SGLT2-inhibitors, demeclocycline, amphotericin, plus OTCs, supplements, caffeine, alcohol, smoking, psychiatric history, head trauma, meningitis, neurosurgery, family history of DI, snoring/apnea, and lower urinary tract/prostate symptoms.
3. Repeat office urinalysis with microscopy and reflex urine culture; if dysuria, discharge or risk factors add nucleic acid amplification test for Neisseria gonorrhoeae/Chlamydia trachomatis. Perform genital/prostate exam and bladder post-void residual scan; do not retreat for UTI without culture.
4. Refer outpatient to endocrinology within 2-4 weeks, nephrology if unavailable, for supervised water-deprivation test with desmopressin challenge or hypertonic saline-stimulated plasma copeptin to distinguish central DI vs nephrogenic DI vs primary polydipsia. Advise against unsupervised fluid restriction at home and against empiric desmopressin, thiazides, or NSAIDs.
5. If testing shows central DI, then obtain MRI sella with gadolinium and 8am anterior pituitary labs: TSH with reflex free T4, cortisol with ACTH, LH, FSH, total testosterone, prolactin, IGF-1. If nephrogenic DI, evaluate reversible causes including lithium level only if exposed, CKD, obstruction, sickle screen if indicated. If polyuria not confirmed, refer to urology for overactive bladder/prostatitis evaluation.
6. Counsel to drink to thirst with free water access, avoid excess caffeine/alcohol, avoid overdrinking, and bring diary to specialist; explain water-deprivation testing requires monitoring to avoid severe dehydration.
7. Return precautions: seek urgent care for confusion, syncope, severe dizziness, vomiting/fever preventing fluid intake, unquenchable thirst with markedly increased output, or inability to keep up with losses.

High-frequency episodic migraine without aura with chronification and work disability — 8-hour left-sided headaches 8-12 days/month with photophobia/nausea — without red flags or focal deficits; remote sports-related TBIs alone do not indicate secondary headache.

1. Document BP, complete neurologic exam including fundoscopy, cranial nerves, motor/sensory, coordination/gait; do not order routine labs, EEG, CT, or MRI now — reserve MRI brain without contrast for abnormal exam, new red flags, or atypical treatment-resistant course.
2. Stop concurrent aspirin plus ibuprofen — explain increased GI bleed/renal risk without added benefit; avoid opioids, butalbital, and daily NSAIDs; limit acute use to <10 days/month for triptans and <15 days/month for NSAIDs to prevent medication-overuse headache.
3. Start sumatriptan 100 mg PO at headache onset, may repeat 100 mg once after 2 hours if incomplete relief, max 200 mg/24h; first screen for coronary disease, stroke/TIA, uncontrolled hypertension, peripheral vascular disease, hemiplegic migraine or brainstem aura; counsel on transient chest tightness/pressure, flushing, paresthesias.
4. Start prevention given 8-12 disabling days/month: propranolol LA 80 mg daily if no asthma/COPD, HR <60, hypotension, or severe depression, titrate to 120-160 mg daily as tolerated for an 8-12 week trial to assess for ≥50% reduction in headache days; monitor HR/BP; counsel on fatigue, dizziness, bradycardia, sexual dysfunction, mood lowering.
5. Provide headache diary — date, duration, severity, associated symptoms, triggers, acute meds/response, disability days — and counsel on regular sleep schedule, daily aerobic exercise, hydration, limiting caffeine and alcohol, not skipping meals, stress management.
6. Screen for depression/anxiety, insomnia/sleep apnea/snoring, cognitive concerns or mood lability related to prior TBIs, alcohol, caffeine, and supplement use; treat comorbidities that drive chronification.
7. Refer routinely to neurology in 2-3 months for diagnostic confirmation and preventive management; schedule PCP follow-up in 4-6 weeks to review diary, efficacy, HR/BP, adherence and side effects; if inadequate response after adequate trial, neurology to consider alternative preventive or CGRP-targeted therapy.
8. Seek urgent care for thunderclap/worst-ever headache, new focal weakness/numbness, speech/vision change, confusion, seizure, fever with neck stiffness, syncope, head trauma, or headache >72 hours despite treatment; obtain prompt MRI brain without contrast if any develop.

DWI-negative probable left-hemisphere high-risk TIA presenting ~8 days after event, still within the high early-recurrence window but outside the proven 24-hour window for dual antiplatelet initiation.

1. Obtain urgent large-vessel imaging within 24-48 hours: CTA head and neck with contrast, or carotid duplex plus MRA head/neck if contrast/renal contraindication, to exclude symptomatic left carotid stenosis.
2. Complete cardioembolic workup: 12-lead ECG now and transthoracic echocardiogram; continue current 7-day Zio patch - if negative but no cause found, extend to 14-day monitor per neurology.
3. Obtain fasting lipid panel, hemoglobin A1c, CBC, basic metabolic panel with eGFR, urinalysis for proteinuria, and BNP given trace pedal edema; review meds for amlodipine, pioglitazone, NSAIDs that cause edema.
4. Stop clopidogrel 75 mg - DAPT benefit shown only when started within 24 hours of minor stroke/high-risk TIA; starting at day 7-8 increases bleeding without proven benefit in a 77-year-old. Continue aspirin 81 mg daily alone, avoid NSAIDs.
5. Start high-intensity statin for secondary prevention: atorvastatin 40 mg daily, check baseline LFTs; continue long-term regardless of LDL.
6. Optimize vascular risk factors in primary care in 1-2 weeks: confirm home BP control targeting <130/80 long-term without acute aggressive lowering, review diabetes regimen to avoid hypoglycemia/hypotension, reinforce smoking cessation if applicable, Mediterranean diet, and daily activity as tolerated.
7. Refer urgently to neurology/stroke clinic within 7 days; if CTA shows ipsilateral carotid stenosis 70-99%, refer urgently to vascular surgery/neurointerventional for carotid endarterectomy/stenting within 2 weeks of event; if atrial fibrillation/flutter on ECG/Zio or intracardiac thrombus on echo, stop antiplatelet and start oral anticoagulation per cardiology/neurology.
8. Counsel: TIA is a warning for stroke - call 911 for FAST symptoms, do not drive until neurology clears; seek urgent care for recurrent unilateral weakness, speech change, vision loss, severe headache, or aspirin bleeding - black stools, hematuria, prolonged bleeding.

Resolving post-infectious bronchiolitis with new but now asymptomatic right lower lobe tree-in-bud nodularity, bronchial wall thickening and mucus plugging after self-limited cough, likely post-viral/bacterial and not active NTM/TB, ABPA/vasculitis, or malignancy; scattered truncal keratoses are age-typical, not eruptive Leser-Trelat.

1. Do not prescribe antibiotics, systemic corticosteroids, antifungals, and do not obtain sputum bacterial culture, sputum AFB smear/culture, PET-CT, bronchoscopy or biopsy while asymptomatic.
2. Obtain repeat thin-section noncontrast CT chest in 3 months to document resolution; have chest radiologist re-review index scan for endobronchial lesion/central obstruction and extent of bronchiectasis. If resolved, resume routine annual lung cancer screening; if persistent, progressive, or new bronchiectasis/cavitation, refer routinely to pulmonology within 4 weeks for NTM/ABPA evaluation.
3. Take focused history at next primary care visit: TB contacts, travel/birth origin, prior TB, hot-tub/sauna exposure, dysphagia, witnessed aspiration, reflux, wheeze/asthma/atopy, new medications/supplements, alcohol use, and fevers, productive cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, weight loss, night sweats, sinus disease, neuropathy, rash; review vital signs, lung exam, lymphadenopathy.
4. Review prior CBCs with differential to document absolute eosinophil count and stability; defer total serum IgE, Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG, spirometry with bronchodilator, ANCA, stool ova and parasites, or other eosinophilia workup unless infiltrate persists on repeat CT, respiratory symptoms recur, or AEC is >1500 cells/mcL, rising, or with systemic features.
5. Reassure that scattered stable seborrheic keratoses do not warrant tumor markers, CT abdomen/pelvis, endoscopy, or urgent dermatology; continue age-appropriate cancer screening, reinforce continued smoking abstinence, and optimize glycemic control. No isolation needed.
6. Return precautions: seek prompt care for cough >8 weeks, fever, purulent sputum, hemoptysis, dyspnea, chest pain, weight loss, or night sweats, which should prompt earlier repeat imaging and pulmonology referral.

Persistent confusion with new delusions/paranoia 2 months after CABG-related delirium in an older adult with vascular disease and no prior psychiatric/dementia history suggests prolonged delirium versus incident major neurocognitive disorder with secondary psychosis, requiring structured collateral, delirium/cognitive assessment and reversible-cause evaluation with safety planning.

1. Obtain detailed collateral from wife with patient present: premorbid baseline, onset/course/fluctuation and inattention, sleep-wake reversal, fever, dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, edema, urinary symptoms, constipation, pain, alcohol/benzodiazepine/opioid/OTC/antihistamine/sleep-aid use, all pill bottles, adherence, ADLs/IADLs, and behavioral/safety events.
2. Perform standardized in-clinic assessment: Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) for delirium, PHQ-9 for depression, orthostatic vitals and pulse oximetry, plus screen for suicidal/homicidal ideation, agitation, driving, cooking, electrical/power-tool use, firearms, wandering, and decision-making capacity.
3. Complete medication/substance reconciliation including anticholinergic burden, sedatives, opioids, muscle relaxants, and alcohol; taper/discontinue deliriogenic agents where possible, correct sensory impairment, dehydration, sleep deprivation, and immobility.
4. Order CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, TSH with reflex to free T4, and vitamin B12; obtain ECG for ischemia/arrhythmia/atrial fibrillation. Obtain urinalysis with microscopy and reflex culture, chest evaluation, and infection/hypoxia workup only if CAM-positive, febrile, or with urinary/respiratory symptoms.
5. Review post-CABG status: anemia, acute kidney injury, heart failure/low output, hypotension, hypoxia, sleep apnea, and pain; optimize perfusion, oxygenation, hydration, sleep-wake cycle, mobilization, and cardiac follow-up.
6. Counsel that post-CABG cognitive dysfunction can persist months but new paranoia/delusions are not expected and need evaluation; advise 24-hour supervision, no driving or unsupervised electrical work/power tools, no alcohol/sedatives, structured routine, fall precautions, and supervised medications until cleared.
7. Refer to geriatrics or neurology memory clinic in 2-4 weeks for formal neuropsychological testing if MoCA abnormal or deficit persists, and to psychiatry within 1-2 weeks for new delusions/paranoia — urgent/same-day if unsafe, agitated, or suicidal/homicidal; do not start routine antipsychotic or benzodiazepine in clinic given CAD/elderly risk.
8. Defer repeat head CT and routine MRI brain, EEG, or extensive dementia biomarkers now given recent noncontrast CT with no acute infarct and normal neuro exam; pursue MRI brain without contrast only if new focal deficit, head trauma on antiplatelet/anticoagulation, rapid decline, or neurology advises. Recheck in primary care in 1-2 weeks with wife.
9. Return precautions: seek urgent/ED care for worsening confusion/inattention, agitation, hallucinations, suicidal/homicidal thoughts, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, fever, focal weakness, speech change, head injury, or loss of safe supervision; if CAM-positive, evaluate urgently for medical precipitant.

Recurrent prolonged productive cough after viral illness in a functionally fit older adult with normal CXR suggests underlying chronic airway disease such as chronic bronchitis/bronchiectasis or post-viral airway inflammation rather than repeated acute bacterial bronchitis; transient response to azithromycin likely reflects anti-inflammatory effect, not cure, and repeated use risks resistance, QT arrhythmia, hearing loss, and C. difficile.

1. Do not continue empiric azithromycin for each cough episode. Reserve antibiotics for signs of bacterial exacerbation — increased sputum purulence plus increased volume and/or increased dyspnea, fever, or pneumonia findings — and obtain sputum before prescribing.
2. Take focused interval history and exam: smoking pack-years and vaping, occupational/dust exposures, ACE-inhibitor use, sputum volume/color change, hemoptysis, sinus congestion/postnasal drip, wheeze, reflux/heartburn/regurgitation, weight loss, fevers, prior sputum cultures, and vaccination history; record vitals, pulse oximetry, sinus and lung exam, and exercise tolerance.
3. Review pending PFTs with pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry with lung volumes; do not start inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting bronchodilator or systemic steroids without obstruction or wheeze/asthma evidence.
4. Obtain high-resolution CT chest without contrast to evaluate for bronchiectasis, airway wall thickening, mucus plugging, or nodules. During next productive episode, obtain expectorated sputum for Gram stain and routine aerobic bacterial culture before antibiotics; if CT shows bronchiectasis, add sputum AFB smear and mycobacterial culture and refer before any macrolide monotherapy.
5. Do not escalate GERD therapy for cough alone: continue famotidine as needed, do not restart PPI without typical reflux symptoms since PPIs already tried without cough relief; continue daily walking, adequate hydration, smoking cessation and irritant avoidance if relevant, and verify age-appropriate vaccines — annual influenza, pneumococcal per CDC ≥65, RSV, updated COVID-19, and Tdap if not current.
6. Refer to outpatient pulmonology in 4-6 weeks with PFTs and CT results. If CT confirms bronchiectasis, pulmonology to direct airway clearance, repeat cultures, and consider long-term macrolide only after exclusion of nontuberculous mycobacteria plus baseline ECG for QTc, hearing screen, LFTs, and drug-interaction review; if PFTs show persistent airflow obstruction, manage as COPD per GOLD.
7. Counsel that post-viral productive cough often lasts 3-8 weeks without bacterial infection. Seek sooner care for hemoptysis, fever >101F persistent >3 days, worsening dyspnea, chest pain, weight loss, or inability to complete usual 2-mile walk.

Grade 3 nivolumab infusion reaction with hemodynamic instability, cutaneous, GI and vasomotor features now resolved, in BRAF-mutant metastatic melanoma with limited options requesting rechallenge.

1. Hold nivolumab and do not give the scheduled dose in routine outpatient infusion: Grade 3 infusion reaction is a labeled indication for permanent discontinuation, so routine rechallenge is unsafe; any further dose is an exception only if medical oncology and allergy agree benefit outweighs risk of fatal anaphylaxis/cytokine release, with documented informed consent.
2.
