Arrange urgent medical oncology within 1 week and urgent allergy/immunology/drug desensitization within 1 week, before any dosing decision, to phenotype reaction, assess cross-reactivity to other anti-PD-1 agents including pembrolizumab, and determine if desensitization in a tertiary center is feasible; do not empirically switch to pembrolizumab without allergy guidance.
3. Retrieve and review cycle 3 infusion record: timing relative to infusion start/end, rate, premedications, concomitant dabrafenib/trametinib and anti-seizure drug timing, full vitals/telemetry, oxygen saturation, ECG monitoring, and ED/clinic notes to exclude sepsis, arrhythmia, acute coronary event, or BRAF/MEK toxicity as contributors.
4. Evaluate now for stability and rechallenge risk with focused exam including orthostatic vitals and pulse oximetry, 12-lead ECG, and medication reconciliation for agents that worsen anaphylaxis or mask prodrome; do not obtain delayed serum tryptase, echo, stress testing, restaging scans, or routine labs now unless new symptoms or ECG abnormality dictate. Continue dabrafenib/trametinib and anti-seizure therapy per oncology/neurology without interruption.
5. If allergy/oncology approve a trial rechallenge, give only as inpatient or tertiary desensitization unit with ICU backup, continuous vitals, IV access, resuscitation drugs/airway support available, allergy-directed desensitization/slow-titration protocol with extended post-infusion observation, and paired serum tryptase protocol for future event (acute 30 min to 3 hours plus baseline >24 hours); do not attempt rechallenge with only standard premedication and slower rate in community clinic.
6. Counsel that recurrence risk is high and may be more rapid/severe, confirm goals of care given stage IV disease, advise to seek emergency care for dyspnea, chest pain, dizziness/syncope, palpitations, rash, facial/lip swelling, wheeze, vomiting/diarrhea, or rigors/fever, and to bring infusion reaction history to all providers.

Atypical for checkpoint pneumonitis; diffuse bronchial wall thickening with tree-in-bud in a patient with prior positive Quantiferon and prolonged corticosteroids is concerning for active mycobacterial bronchiolitis, most urgently TB reactivation, and empiric steroids would be unsafe.

1. Do NOT restart prednisone or other systemic corticosteroids and do not provide a taper at this time; contact oncology promptly to hold checkpoint immunotherapy pending workup.
2. Place in airborne precautions immediately and evaluate urgently today with vitals including SpO2, lung exam, and assessment for hypoxia, hemoptysis, or respiratory distress; admit if hypoxic, unstable, or unable to isolate safely as outpatient.
3. Obtain 3 sputum specimens 8-24 hours apart including one early-morning for AFB smear, mycobacterial culture, and MTB NAAT with Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, plus sputum bacterial Gram stain and culture, respiratory viral PCR panel, HIV-1/2 Ag/Ab if status unknown, and compare current CT chest to all priors.
4. Refer urgently within 24-72 hours to infectious disease and pulmonology; if unable to expectorate or smears negative but suspicion remains, proceed to bronchoscopy with BAL for AFB smear, MTB NAAT, mycobacterial/bacterial/fungal cultures, Nocardia and PJP PCR as directed by consultants.
5. Retrieve records of LTBI evaluation/treatment 7 years ago, prior AFB results, prior chest imaging, all steroid doses/durations and PJP prophylaxis, cancer therapy, diabetes, exposures, travel, and TB contacts; avoid empiric fluoroquinolones which can mask TB and promote resistance unless directed by ID.
6. Counsel to wear surgical mask, stay home from work/public, cough etiquette, and household contacts to seek care if symptomatic; maintain airborne isolation until active TB excluded per infection control.
7. If MTB NAAT or smears positive, maintain isolation, notify public health/infection control, and start multidrug TB therapy only under ID supervision; if alternative bacterial infection confirmed, treat per cultures and only reconsider steroids with ID/pulmonology/oncology if noninfectious pneumonitis proven.
8. Return precautions: seek urgent care for worsening dyspnea, hypoxia, chest pain, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, or weight loss; close follow-up in 2-3 days pending smear/NAAT results.

Chronic migratory pruritic wheals for 6 weeks consistent with chronic urticaria, likely chronic spontaneous urticaria, without described anaphylaxis, persistent lesions, or systemic features of vasculitis.

1. Continue prophylactic second-generation H1-antihistamine daily, not PRN: cetirizine 10 mg PO once daily taken consistently even when clear for at least 4 weeks. Alternatives if sedated: loratadine 10 mg daily or fexofenadine 180 mg daily. Counsel mild sedation, dry mouth, urinary hesitancy; use caution driving and with alcohol.
2. Stop routine diphenhydramine for control or rescue due to sedation, impaired driving/work performance, anticholinergic effects and short duration; do not use chronically, especially in daytime or before driving.
3. Avoid common exacerbating cofactors: NSAIDs including ibuprofen/naproxen/aspirin, excess alcohol, overheating/hot showers, friction/scratching, tight pressure/clothing, sleep deprivation/stress, and acute viral illness. No empiric food elimination, detergent change, or antihistamine holiday needed without clear pattern.
4. Counsel on course and self-monitoring: individual wheals should resolve <24 hours without scarring; disease often persists months to years then remits, antihistamines suppress symptoms but do not cure, and it is not contagious or proof of food allergy. Mark one wheal with pen, note duration, itch vs pain/burning, residual bruise/pigment, take photos, and keep brief diary of medications, illness, pressure/heat/exercise, alcohol/NSAIDs.
5. No routine allergy workup now: no food-specific IgE panels, total IgE, skin-prick testing, or skin biopsy given classic history and no red flags. No routine CBC/CRP/TSH/ANA/complements unless atypical course or vasculitis suspected.
6. Escalate stepwise if not controlled after 2-4 weeks adherent daily therapy: PCP may up-titrate same agent up to 4x standard dose if tolerated, e.g., cetirizine 10 mg BID then up to 20 mg BID, monitoring sedation. If still uncontrolled after 4-6 weeks on high-dose, or needing repeated steroids, refer routinely to allergy/dermatology in 4-8 weeks for add-on omalizumab; do not start chronic systemic steroids, cyclosporine, or dapsone in primary care. Reserve short steroid burst only for severe flare, e.g., prednisone 0.5 mg/kg daily for 3-5 days.
7. Refer promptly to dermatology within 1-2 weeks for punch biopsy and systemic evaluation for urticarial vasculitis if lesions persist >24 hours in same spot, are painful/burning rather than itchy, leave purpura/bruise/hyperpigmentation, or accompanied by fever, arthralgia, abdominal pain, hematuria, or elevated CRP/ESR.
8. Return precautions: seek urgent/ED care for lip/tongue/face swelling, dyspnea, wheeze, dysphagia, dizziness/syncope, or painful persistent purpuric lesions with fever/joint pain. Follow up with PCP in 2-4 weeks to assess control.

Uncomplicated-appearing TMP-SMX hypersensitivity with urticaria/pruritus plus concurrent AKI with dark urine in a patient with baseline CKD from IgA nephropathy, most consistent with hypersensitivity-related kidney injury such as acute interstitial nephritis rather than isolated TMP-related creatinine bump.

1. Document TMP-SMX as drug allergy with reaction “hives/pruritus and acute kidney injury” in all records, counsel strict lifelong avoidance of TMP-SMX and other sulfonamide antibiotics, provide written allergy list, and advise prior 6-month tolerance 10 years ago does not protect against new sensitization.
2. Do not order sulfa skin testing, patch testing, or serum IgE for TMP-SMX, and do not rechallenge or attempt desensitization in primary care; diagnosis is clinical and tests are unvalidated with poor predictive value and risk of harm.
3. Confirm renal recovery and screen for systemic hypersensitivity with: basic metabolic panel with eGFR and potassium/bicarbonate, CBC with differential for eosinophilia, hepatic panel, and urinalysis with microscopy plus spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio compared to IgA nephropathy baseline; do not order urine eosinophils or kidney biopsy in primary care.
4. If dark urine, jaundice, pallor or anemia present, add hemolysis workup: CBC, reticulocyte count, LDH, haptoglobin, total/indirect bilirubin, and creatine kinase for rhabdomyolysis; otherwise do not pursue extensive hemolysis or G6PD testing without clinical clues.
5. Arrange routine nephrology follow-up within 2-4 weeks given doubling of creatinine on CKD, persistent risk of CKD progression/proteinuria, and diabetes insipidus-related volume depletion risk; reinforce hydration, avoid NSAIDs/aminoglycosides/iodinated contrast if possible, and review diabetes insipidus medications and volume status.
6. Refer to allergy non-urgently for education and planning, not for testing: counsel that sulfonamide non-antibiotics such as thiazides, furosemide, celecoxib are usually tolerated despite sulfonamide-antibiotic allergy but should only be started with shared decision-making; if a sulfonamide antibiotic is ever considered essential, it must only be in an allergist-supervised setting.
7. For recurrent UTIs, obtain urine culture with susceptibilities before all treatment, never use TMP-SMX for empiric therapy or prophylaxis, and use culture-directed alternatives per nephrology/urology input; refer routinely to urology for recurrent UTI evaluation coordinated with nephrology given CKD.
8. Return precautions: seek urgent care for facial/lip swelling, dyspnea, wheeze, throat tightness, dizziness, blistering rash, mucosal sores, fever, lymphadenopathy, oliguria, edema, gross hematuria/dark urine recurrence, or rash with hepatitis symptoms.

Symptomatic daily palpitations with only a single very brief remote device-detected AF episode and currently in sinus rhythm suggests possible paroxysmal AF versus non-AF cause such as thyroid over-replacement, with low-intermediate stroke risk and no indication for empiric pre-ablation anticoagulation.

1. Do not start a DOAC or aspirin now in anticipation of ablation — a 75-second episode 1 year ago does not establish clinical AF requiring long-term anticoagulation, and ablation only requires uninterrupted anticoagulation for ≥3 weeks immediately pre-procedure or pre-procedure TEE, to be timed by electrophysiology.
2. Formalize stroke vs bleeding risk to guide shared decision-making if AF is confirmed: recheck BP and history for hypertension, diabetes, heart failure, vascular disease, prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism, bleeding history, renal/liver disease, alcohol use, falls/frailty, and use of NSAIDs, antiplatelets, SSRIs.
3. Obtain 12-lead ECG in clinic, and do not duplicate transthoracic echocardiogram if cardiology will order it — ensure cardiology considers TTE for LA size, LV function, and valvular disease given suspected paroxysmal AF.
4. Order extended continuous ambulatory rhythm monitoring to correlate daily symptoms, e.g., 14-day Zio Patch, rather than 24-48 hour Holter; continue routine cardiology referral in 4-6 weeks given stable sinus rhythm, no syncope, chest pain, or decompensation — no ED referral needed.
5. Order TSH with reflex to free T4 for levothyroxine over-replacement review including dose/adherence, plus CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel with creatinine/eGFR and LFTs for anemia and baseline for potential future anticoagulation, and magnesium; review caffeine, alcohol, decongestants/stimulants, sleep apnea symptoms, and medication list.
6. Counsel on AF modifiable triggers relevant to ablation success and stroke risk: limit alcohol and stimulants/caffeine, maintain healthy weight, treat hypertension and screen/treat obstructive sleep apnea, regular moderate exercise, no smoking; explain that DOACs reduce stroke but increase major bleeding and require adherence without routine INR monitoring.
7. Conditional plan: if monitor documents clinical AF, cardiology to confirm burden and pursue shared decision-making for anticoagulation given CHA2DS2-VA 1 for age 65-74 alone is reasonable but not mandatory (2a indication), and if ablation is planned, initiate uninterrupted DOAC per EP timing rather than now.
8. Follow up in primary care in 2-4 weeks to review monitor, ECG, and labs; seek urgent care sooner for syncope/presyncope, chest pain/pressure, sustained rapid or irregular palpitations, dyspnea, or neurologic symptoms of TIA/stroke such as facial droop, unilateral weakness, or speech change.

Stable exertional substernal pressure with dyspnea in a 50-year-old man with prediabetes, hyperlipidemia and premature family CAD is concerning for stable angina with intermediate pretest probability; a 10-year ASCVD score of 1.2% does not exclude symptomatic obstructive CAD and a single negative functional test does not rule it out, especially if submaximal.

1. Refer to outpatient cardiology within 2-4 weeks for suspected stable angina; do not reassure based on ASCVD score or negative stress test alone, and do not proceed to invasive coronary angiography or repeat functional stress testing as next step given stable symptoms without high-risk features.
2. Obtain coronary CT angiography with IV contrast (not coronary calcium score alone) as next anatomic test per stable chest pain guidelines; check serum creatinine with eGFR for contrast safety, and retrieve prior stress test report including modality, workload/METs and % maximal predicted heart rate achieved, symptoms, ECG changes, and imaging findings to assess adequacy and bring to cardiology.
3. Perform focused history of pain duration, triggers, relief with rest, functional capacity, smoking, blood pressure, and full medication reconciliation for PR-prolonging drugs, plus vitals with heart rate/BP, BMI, cardiac exam for aortic stenosis murmur, lung exam and edema; update fasting lipid panel and hemoglobin A1c if not recent. Isolated asymptomatic 1st-degree AV block needs no pacemaker, Holter, electrophysiology referral, or routine echocardiogram, troponin, or BNP now.
4. Counsel to avoid vigorous exertion that provokes pressure/dyspnea until evaluated but maintain usual daily activity, and that 1st-degree AV block alone needs no treatment/restriction — report syncope, presyncope, palpitations, or marked bradycardia.
5. If CCTA shows obstructive disease — ≥50% left main or ≥70% in other epicardial vessels, or high-risk anatomy — expedite cardiology for invasive angiography and guideline-directed medical therapy; if non-obstructive, continue risk-factor management with cardiology.
6. Seek ED care sooner for rest or prolonged >10-15 min pressure unrelieved by rest, worsening dyspnea at rest, syncope, sustained palpitations, or new exertional intolerance.

Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation of the face following resolved allergic contact dermatitis. At 6 weeks persistence is expected and typically fades over months, with UV/visible light and ongoing inflammation as main drivers of persistence.

1. Confirm PIH clinically without biopsy or labs: document distribution with photos, Fitzpatrick type, and absence of active dermatitis — no scale, erythema, vesicles, or itch. If active eczema, papules/plaques beyond pigment, rapid spread, or diagnostic uncertainty, hold lightening therapy and seek routine dermatology.
2. Institute strict daily photoprotection, the cornerstone of therapy especially on acetazolamide: broad-spectrum tinted SPF 50+ with iron oxides for UV + visible light, nickel-sized amount to face each morning, reapply every 2 hours outdoors, plus wide-brim hat and midday shade. Continue acetazolamide for idiopathic intracranial hypertension; do not stop for pigmentation.
3. Use gentle skincare and prevent recurrence: fragrance-free cleanser and moisturizer, no scrubs, peels, picking, or fragranced/bleaching products; avoid prolonged topical steroids on face; identify and avoid the contact allergen that triggered the rash — refer routinely for patch testing if trigger unknown.
4. Start azelaic acid 15% gel thin layer to hyperpigmented areas BID, safe first-line for face and safe in pregnancy/breastfeeding. Warn of mild stinging/irritation initially; use with moisturizer and sunscreen.
5. If not pregnant, breastfeeding, or planning pregnancy within treatment period — verify with urine hCG and contraception counseling — add tretinoin 0.025% cream pea-sized to full face at night 2-3x/week, titrate to nightly as tolerated. Counsel: irritation, peeling and initial darkening can occur, increases sun sensitivity, teratogenic; hold if eczema recurs or severe irritation and resume at lower frequency with moisturizer buffering.
6. Defer hydroquinone 4%, triple-combination cream, chemical peels, and laser to routine dermatology in 8-12 weeks if persistent despite 1-5; do not initiate lasers/peels in primary care or while inflamed, and avoid prolonged unsupervised hydroquinone or potent steroids due to ochronosis, atrophy, and rebound PIH, particularly in medium-dark skin. Counsel fading takes 3-12 months and requires continuous protection and adherence.
7. Return sooner for recurrence of itch, redness, scaling, blistering, pigment spreading rapidly despite protection, or signs of irritation from topicals.

Severe hypercholesterolemia with LDL 200 mg/dL in a 34-year-old man, concerning for familial hypercholesterolemia and high lifetime ASCVD risk. Recent palpitations/tachycardia appear transient in context of sleep deprivation/jet lag with negative workup so far, but need confirmation of resolution and cardiac stability.

1. Confirm persistent severe hypercholesterolemia: obtain repeat lipid panel with total cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C, triglycerides, and non-HDL-C; review diet, alcohol, medications/supplements that raise LDL (e.g., thiazides, corticosteroids, antipsychotics, isotretinoin, anabolic steroids).
2. Focused FH and ASCVD risk assessment: detailed personal history of ASCVD, smoking/vaping, hypertension, diabetes, diet, physical activity, BMI, and family history of LDL >190-250 and premature ASCVD (<55y men, <65y women) or sudden death; exam for tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma, corneal arcus under age 45; obtain baseline ALT/AST before statin. Do not repeat TSH, A1c, or troponin if asymptomatic.
3. Start high-intensity statin given LDL ≥190 mg/dL: e.g., atorvastatin 40 mg daily or rosuvastatin 20 mg daily long-term, with shared decision-making targeting ≥50% LDL reduction. Counsel that therapy is typically lifelong, report unexplained severe muscle pain/weakness, dark urine, jaundice, and avoid excess alcohol and check for CYP3A4 interactions with atorvastatin.
4. Intensive lifestyle modification with registered dietitian referral: Mediterranean or DASH pattern, reduce saturated fat to <6-7% calories and eliminate trans fat, increase soluble fiber, maintain healthy weight, ≥150 min/week moderate aerobic activity plus resistance training 2x/week, limit alcohol, stop tobacco if used, and sleep hygiene for jet lag recovery.
5. Evaluate for familial hypercholesterolemia and cascade screening: apply Dutch Lipid Clinic criteria; recommend lipid screening for all first-degree relatives and partner/children per guidelines. If LDL persistently >250, physical stigmata, or strong family history, refer to lipidology/genetics for FH confirmation and consideration of genetic testing; do not add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor initially — add via specialist only if inadequate response on maximal statin at 4-12 week recheck.
6. Address index palpitations: review ED ECG, vitals, and troponin; check heart rate/rhythm and obtain resting 12-lead ECG at this visit. If now asymptomatic with normal exam and ECG, no further cardiac testing; advise avoidance of caffeine, energy drinks, alcohol, nicotine, decongestants/stimulants and address stress/sleep. If recurrent palpitations, chest pain, syncope, dyspnea, or abnormal ECG, obtain 14-day ambulatory patch/event monitor and refer to cardiology non-urgently.
7. Follow-up in 4-12 weeks with repeat lipid panel, ALT, adherence and side-effect check, then every 3-12 months once stable; return sooner for sustained palpitations, chest pain/pressure, syncope, dyspnea, recurrent arm numbness/neck tightness, or statin intolerance symptoms.

Acute symmetric painful palmar-plantar erythema, swelling, cracking and edema on daily capecitabine is most consistent with capecitabine-induced palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (hand-foot syndrome), not cellulitis or primary inflammatory arthritis. Systemic prednisone does not treat the toxicity and poses high risk at age 82 with HTN, CAD, and CKD.

1. Do not start oral prednisone — risk of hypertension, fluid retention, hyperglycemia, fall, infection masking, and impaired wound healing outweighs any benefit for hand-foot syndrome.
2. Hold capecitabine pending urgent oncology guidance and contact oncology within 24 hours for suspected grade 2-3 hand-foot syndrome; do not start, stop, or dose-adjust oxaliplatin independently, and do not administer further capecitabine until oncology grades toxicity and plans dose interruption/reduction.
3. Assess severity now: temperature, BP, weight, cardiopulmonary and skin exam for blisters, ulceration, moist desquamation, pus, unilateral leg redness/swelling, and impact on walking, grasping, and ADLs; obtain CBC with differential and basic metabolic panel given active chemotherapy, CKD, and edema; defer skin biopsy, joint x-rays, autoimmune panels, and cultures in this symmetric afebrile presentation.
4. Provide supportive skin care: thick bland emollient to hands/feet BID e.g., petrolatum or urea 10% cream, cool compresses, elevation of feet, cushioned footwear, cotton socks/gloves, avoid hot water, friction, pressure, prolonged standing, and tight shoes; continue pantoprazole as symptoms antedated it.
5. Control pain without NSAIDs or steroids given CKD, CAD, age: acetaminophen 500-1000 mg q6h PRN, max 3 g/24 hours, if no liver disease and no excess alcohol use.
6. Counsel that hand-foot syndrome typically improves within 1-2 weeks of holding capecitabine, but oncology often restarts at reduced dose once resolved to grade 0-1; keep hands/feet cool, moist, and protected, and report lack of improvement.
7. Recheck in PCP in 2-3 days for pain, swelling, skin breakdown, BP, weight, and edema; if no improvement 1-2 weeks after hold, refer to dermatology promptly and consider rheumatology for RS3PE/paraneoplastic synovitis mimic.
8. Return precautions: seek urgent care for fever, spreading unilateral redness/warmth, blistering, ulceration, drainage, inability to walk or use hands, rapidly worsening swelling, shortness of breath, chest pain, or unilateral calf pain/swelling.

Rapid eruption of multiple seborrheic keratoses over 4 months at age 57 is not normal aging and is concerning for Leser-Trelat sign, a possible paraneoplastic syndrome most often linked to GI adenocarcinoma as well as breast and lung cancers.

1. Refer urgently to dermatology within 1-2 weeks for full-body skin exam and shave/punch biopsy of a representative new or atypical lesion to confirm seborrheic keratosis and exclude melanoma or pigmented basal cell carcinoma; do not cryoablate, curette, or laser lesions before diagnosis.
2. Perform focused malignancy history and exam now: weight loss, appetite, dysphagia, abdominal pain, bowel habit change, rectal bleeding/melena, prolonged cough, hemoptysis, breast lump/nipple change, postmenopausal bleeding, night sweats, fever, lymphadenopathy, smoking pack-years, family cancer history, and complete breast, lung, abdominal, lymph node and pelvic exam.
3. Expedite age-appropriate cancer screening if not current: screening mammography, colonoscopy, cervical screening per guidelines; obtain now CBC with differential, CMP, and fecal immunochemical test (FIT) to evaluate for anemia, GI blood loss, or hepatic involvement; do not order broad tumor markers such as CEA, CA 19-9, or CA-125 for screening.
4. Obtain PA and lateral chest x-ray now given smoking history, COPD, and lung cancer association; if x-ray abnormal, systemic symptoms, anemia, FIT-positive, or no recent colonoscopy/upper endoscopy, obtain contrast-enhanced CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and refer promptly to gastroenterology for EGD and colonoscopy.
5. Counsel that Leser-Trelat association is debated and may be coincidental but cannot be dismissed as normal; advise lesions themselves are benign and need no removal unless symptomatic, avoid picking/scratching, and report pruritus, bleeding, ulceration, rapid growth or color change; offer smoking cessation with behavioral counseling plus pharmacotherapy option, e.g., combination nicotine patch plus lozenge, varenicline, or bupropion SR per preference/contraindications, and optimize COPD care.
6. Follow up in primary care in 2-4 weeks to review pathology, labs, imaging and screening completion; if malignancy found refer urgently to oncology and relevant specialty; if workup negative, maintain close clinical surveillance for 6-12 months for emerging symptoms.
7. Return precautions: seek prompt care for unintentional weight loss, persistent abdominal pain, vomiting, dysphagia, GI bleeding or black stools, cough >2-3 weeks, hemoptysis, new breast lump, enlarging lymph nodes, persistent fever, or rapidly changing skin lesion.

Persistent mild fasting hyperprolactinemia in a 40-year-old man with erectile dysfunction and no mass-effect symptoms or drug cause. Microprolactinoma is possible but secondary causes and biologically inactive macroprolactin must be excluded before attributing symptoms to prolactin.

1. Perform focused exam and history review: blood pressure, BMI, confrontation visual fields, breast for galactorrhea/gynecomastia, testicular size/mass, libido, morning erections, fertility plans, cardiovascular risks, depression/sleep, and re-confirm no antipsychotics, metoclopramide/prochlorperazine, verapamil, opioids, antidepressants, H2-blockers, herbal/testosterone supplements, chest-wall irritation, recent strenuous exercise, stress or nipple stimulation.
2. Obtain secondary-cause labs: TSH with reflex to free T4, basic metabolic panel with creatinine/eGFR, and 8-10 AM fasting total testosterone with LH and FSH on two mornings; do not start testosterone replacement or dopamine agonist before workup complete.
3. Obtain polyethylene glycol precipitation test for macroprolactin / monomeric prolactin fraction, given only mild elevation 27-30 ng/mL; if predominantly macroprolactin and testosterone/LH/FSH, TSH and creatinine normal, prolactinoma is unlikely.
4. If TSH and creatinine normal and true monomeric hyperprolactinemia persists, order routine outpatient dedicated MRI sella/pituitary with gadolinium pituitary protocol within 4-8 weeks, not urgent brain MRI/CT without pituitary cuts; no emergency imaging needed absent headache, vision change, or diplopia.
5. Refer to endocrinology non-urgently in 4-8 weeks for hyperprolactinemia management; if MRI shows adenoma ≥10 mm, lesion abutting optic chiasm, or multiple pituitary deficits, add formal Humphrey visual fields, IGF-1, 8 AM cortisol/ACTH, TSH/free T4, LH/FSH/testosterone panel, and urgent neuro-ophthalmology and pituitary neurosurgery referral.
6. Counsel that prolactin should be drawn fasting, rested, morning, avoiding exercise, sexual activity, alcohol excess, and nipple/chest stimulation for 24 hours prior; explain mild hyperprolactinemia can lower libido/testosterone and cause ED/infertility but ED is often multifactorial and needs cardiovascular/diabetes review.
7. Return precautions: seek prompt care for new headache, vision loss/double vision, visual field cut, galactorrhea, breast enlargement, marked libido loss, or infertility.

Short-course oral alendronate for osteopenia in a 78-year-old at high fracture risk who now needs invasive dentoalveolar surgery. One year exposure without glucocorticoids or other MRONJ risk factors makes MRONJ risk extremely low, while interruption increases fracture risk.

1. Continue alendronate through the procedure — do not hold before and do not delay surgery for a drug holiday; maintain current weekly schedule on time.
2. Coordinate directly with the dentist, preferably an experienced oral and maxillofacial surgeon: disclose alendronate dose/duration and osteopenia/high fracture risk status, discuss staged extraction with delayed graft/implant vs immediate implant and non-implant alternatives, and document informed consent that MRONJ and implant failure risk is very low (~0.01-0.1% with oral bisphosphonates) but increased with extraction + graft + implant.
3. Do not order serum CTX, other bone turnover markers, or routine labs/imaging to time the procedure — they do not predict MRONJ and should not guide hold/resume decisions.
4. Continue aspirin for TIA secondary prevention and atorvastatin perioperatively — do not stop single-agent aspirin for tooth extraction; use local hemostasis measures and advise dentist of antiplatelet use.
5. Counsel on risk reduction and administration: meticulous oral hygiene and completion of any active dental infection treatment before surgery, avoid tobacco, take alendronate upright with full glass water staying upright 30-60 min, maintain adequate calcium/vitamin D intake, and expect mucosal closure in 4-6 weeks with longer osseous healing for graft/implant.
6. Plan follow-up and contingency: routine dentist wound check in 1-2 weeks until mucosal healing; if surgeon insists on a hold despite guidance, limit to brief interruption only if systemic fracture risk permits and resume promptly after soft-tissue closure in coordination with primary care, not after months; if exposed bone, jaw pain/swelling, purulence, paresthesia, or socket non-healing beyond 2-4 weeks, obtain urgent oral surgery evaluation for MRONJ.
7. Return precautions: seek prompt care for fever, worsening jaw pain/swelling, foul taste/drainage, loose implant, exposed bone, or extraction site that does not progressively improve.

Thin elderly woman with worsening fasting-predominant hyperglycemia and clinically significant recent weight loss to BMI 19.7 on subtherapeutic oral semaglutide, concerning for insulin deficiency/LADA and frailty/osteoporosis risk rather than typical insulin-resistant type 2 diabetes.
GLP-1–induced weight loss and sarcopenia would be harmful here.

1. Do not start dulaglutide or any other GLP-1 receptor agonist; discontinue oral semaglutide 3 mg now — 3 mg is a starter dose, weight loss without GI effects signals unacceptable catabolic effect at low BMI with osteoporosis history.
2. Obtain: hemoglobin A1c, basic metabolic panel with eGFR, LFTs, CBC, TSH with reflex to free T4, vitamin B12, 25-hydroxy vitamin D, fasting C-peptide with concurrent fasting glucose, GAD-65 antibodies, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and review age-appropriate cancer screening (colonoscopy, mammography), smoking history, and systems review for malignancy/hyperthyroidism/malabsorption.
3. Start basal insulin for presumed insulin deficiency and catabolism: insulin glargine U-100 6 units subQ at bedtime, titrate by 2 units every 3 days to fasting 90-130 mg/dL; hold and call if glucose <70 mg/dL or nocturnal hypoglycemia. Continue metformin 1000 mg BID only if eGFR ≥45 and eating adequately; stop or reduce if anorexia, GI intolerance, eGFR <30, or ongoing weight loss.
4. Do not restart pioglitazone — correctly stopped for fracture/bone loss risk; counsel that sitagliptin/DPP-4 inhibitors do not cause osteoporosis, but DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitor are inadequate and inappropriate now due to A1c >8% with weight loss, frailty, and dehydration/fracture risk.
5. Start continuous glucose monitor (or fasting + 2-hour post-meal fingersticks if CGM unavailable), log weights weekly, recheck A1c in 3 months, and follow in 1-2 weeks for insulin titration, hypoglycemia review, and weight check.
6. Refer to endocrinology within 2-4 weeks for LADA evaluation and insulin management; urgent registered dietitian for weight-maintenance, high-protein diet (~1.0-1.2 g/kg/day if renal function normal) plus calcium/vitamin D intake, resistance exercise and fall assessment; obtain DEXA for osteoporosis; ensure annual dilated ophthalmology exam.
7. If GAD-65 positive and/or low C-peptide, treat as LADA/type 1: continue basal, add prandial insulin via endocrinology and DKA education; if weight stabilizes and glycemia improves no pancreatic imaging needed, but if weight loss persists despite stopping semaglutide pursue malignancy/pancreatic workup.
8. Counsel on hypoglycemia signs, driving precautions, insulin injection/storage, and sick-day rules. Seek urgent care for glucose <70 mg/dL not recovering, confusion, sweats/tremor, or nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, fruity breath, polyuria/polydipsia with glucose >250 mg/dL suggesting DKA, or continued weight loss, falls, or fracture.

Persistent iron-deficiency anemia in a 76-year-old anticoagulated man after negative bidirectional endoscopy suggests obscure, likely small-bowel blood loss unmasked by apixaban, with very high stroke risk if anticoagulation is stopped.

1. Continue apixaban without interruption; do not stop or switch to left atrial appendage closure now. CHADS-VASc 5 confers high stroke risk, and Watchman is reserved for absolute contraindication to long-term anticoagulation or life-threatening bleeding despite treatable cause, plus requires post-procedure antithrombotics and carries procedural stroke/bleed risk at this age.
2. Urgently clarify antithrombotic regimen with cardiology, routine within 2-4 weeks: date/type of stents, any concomitant aspirin/clopidogrel/NSAID/SSRI use; if >12 months from stent and stable CAD, stop antiplatelet and continue apixaban monotherapy; verify apixaban dose, creatinine/eGFR, weight, CBC, and drug interactions.
3. Refer to gastroenterology routinely within 4-6 weeks for obscure iron-deficiency workup. Obtain and review last EGD/colonoscopy reports for prep quality, cecal intubation, duodenal biopsies, H. pylori testing, and photos; do not routinely repeat both now if high-quality.
4. Obtain: CBC with differential, reticulocyte count, ferritin, serum iron/TIBC with transferrin saturation, CRP, BMP/eGFR, B12, folate, and tissue transglutaminase-IgA with total IgA if duodenal biopsies not done. Hold oral iron 3-5 days before capsule for visualization.
5. Proceed to video capsule endoscopy as next test if no dysphagia, obstruction symptoms, known stricture/Crohn’s, gastroparesis, or high retention risk — use patency capsule first if risk. If capsule shows small-bowel angioectasia amenable to therapy, refer for device-assisted enteroscopy with argon plasma coagulation; if mass/ulcer/stricture, obtain CT/MR enterography and surgical referral; if negative and anemia persists/recurs, consider repeat high-quality EGD with duodenal biopsies and colonoscopy.
6. Replete iron and recheck CBC/reticulocytes in 4 weeks then ferritin in 8-12 weeks: if mild asymptomatic anemia, ferrous sulfate 325 mg (65 mg elemental) daily or every other day for 3 months; if Hb <9 g/dL, symptomatic, CAD with angina/dyspnea, intolerance, or ongoing loss, give IV iron e.g., ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg IV, repeat in 7 days. Counsel iron causes constipation and dark non-tarry stools, take on empty stomach, avoid with tea/calcium.
7. Return precautions: seek urgent care for melena, hematochezia, hematemesis, hematuria, syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, or worsening fatigue/pallor; do not hold apixaban for minor bruising without cardiology/GI input.

Recurrent hematochezia with change in stool caliber in a 70-year-old with altered colonic anatomy is high-risk for colorectal neoplasia or anastomotic pathology; a normal CT angiogram only excludes brisk active bleeding and does not exclude mucosal mass or intermittent bleeding.

1. Refer urgently to gastroenterology within 2 weeks for complete colonoscopy with intubation of proximal colon and careful evaluation of anastomosis. Do not substitute FIT, flexible sigmoidoscopy, CT colonography, or repeat CT angiography.
2. Obtain outside hospital records: admission Hgb trend and transfusions, vital signs, CT angiography images/report, ECG/echo, discharge medications, especially anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs, iron.
3. See in primary care within 1 week for focused history and exam: stool frequency, caliber change, volume/frequency of hematochezia, melena, weight loss, abdominal pain, vomiting, inability to pass stool/flatus, prior colonoscopy dates and findings, colectomy pathology report, family history of colorectal cancer; abdominal exam, digital rectal exam with anoscopy, orthostatic vitals, and complete medication reconciliation.
4. Order CBC, iron panel with ferritin, and basic metabolic panel for anemia assessment and bowel-prep safety in hypertension, diabetes, and LV dysfunction. Review recent ECG/echocardiogram; coordinate periprocedural sedation risk for LBBB with LV dysfunction with cardiology/anesthesia, and periprocedural holds of antithrombotics and diabetes medications — do not stop cardiac or antithrombotic drugs without coordination.
5. Counsel that stable vitals/Hgb do not rule out cancer, explain bowel-prep hydration and diabetes-medication adjustments, and advise strict avoidance of NSAIDs, alcohol excess, and self-initiated iron without evaluation given PUD and prior GI bleed.
6. Conditional next steps: if mass, high-grade stricture, or inability to complete colonoscopy is found, refer urgently to colorectal surgery and GI oncology; if colonoscopy is negative and bleeding recurs, pursue EGD given PUD/GERD history and then small-bowel evaluation; if obstructive symptoms develop, seek urgent surgical evaluation.
7. Return precautions: seek urgent/ED care for large-volume hematochezia, melena, dizziness/syncope, chest pain/palpitations, dyspnea, severe abdominal pain/distension, vomiting, inability to pass stool/flatus, or fever.

Asymptomatic man with completely resected low-risk adenomas on colonoscopy 1 year ago with 5-year surveillance planned, now with persistent FIT positivity stemming from inappropriate FIT use during prolonged travel-related diarrhea. No family history of colorectal cancer and no current symptoms favors false-positive/benign source over interval neoplasia.

1. Do NOT repeat colonoscopy or order CT colonography now for FIT positivity alone; verify prior colonoscopy was high-quality by reviewing report for adequate bowel prep, documented cecal intubation, and complete polyp resection, and if confirmed maintain 5-year surveillance interval — i.e., repeat colonoscopy in ~4 years.
2. Discontinue interval stool-based testing: do NOT repeat FIT; FIT is not indicated to evaluate acute diarrhea nor for surveillance after adenoma resection.
3. Review for benign FIT confounders: NSAIDs, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, alcohol use, history of hemorrhoids, anal fissure, rectal bleeding, hematuria, and perform focused exam including abdominal exam plus perianal inspection and digital rectal exam; hold nonessential NSAIDs.
4. Obtain complete blood count (CBC) to exclude clinically significant blood loss; if normal and exam unrevealing, obtain no further labs, stool culture, ova and parasites, C. difficile testing, inflammatory markers, CEA, imaging, or EGD now that traveler's diarrhea has resolved. If CBC shows anemia, refer to gastroenterology promptly for expedited evaluation including iron studies with ferritin and repeat colonoscopy planning.
5. Counsel that mother's osteoarthritis does not confer colorectal cancer risk and does not change surveillance or warrant genetics referral; explain FIT detects human globin from lower GI blood and can be positive from hemorrhoids/fissure and during diarrheal illness, and that no diet restriction is needed for FIT.
6. Return precautions and conditional plan: seek sooner care for rectal bleeding, melena, iron-deficiency symptoms, abdominal pain, weight loss, or change in bowel habits or recurrent prolonged diarrhea; if any develop, refer urgently to gastroenterology for early colonoscopy +/- upper GI evaluation.

Stable isolated mild thrombocytopenia (100-150k for 4 years, currently 110k) without bleeding, other cytopenias, or systemic features is not ITP (defined as <100k) and favors pseudothrombocytopenia or a benign stable process with very low bleeding risk.

1. Exclude pseudothrombocytopenia: inspect prior CBCs for trend and obtain CBC with differential with peripheral smear review for platelet clumps, giant platelets, blasts, dysplasia, and RBC/WBC abnormalities, plus repeat platelet count in citrate or heparin tube if clumping or EDTA effect suspected.
2. Take focused bleeding and exposure history and exam: details of postpartum hemorrhage, menses, epistaxis, gum bleeding, hematuria, GI bleeding, surgical/dental bleeding, ISTH bleeding score if indicated, plus all prescription, OTC, supplement, recent infection/vaccine, alcohol use (specifically quinine, TMP-SMX, heparin, anticonvulsants, SSRIs, NSAIDs, antiplatelets), and exam for petechiae, purpura, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, liver disease stigmata.
3. If smear shows no clumps, no giant/small platelets, and no RBC/WBC abnormalities, and exam is normal, do not order further labs, abdominal imaging, bone marrow biopsy, or genetic testing at this time.
4. Do not treat: no corticosteroids, IVIG, anti-D, thrombopoietin-receptor agonists, immunosuppression, splenectomy, or prophylactic platelet transfusion for asymptomatic platelets >100k without bleeding.
5. Monitor in primary care: repeat CBC with differential in 6-12 months and before major surgery, invasive procedure, or pregnancy; refer non-urgently to hematology only if platelets fall <100k, other cytopenias or smear abnormalities develop, significant bleeding occurs, or for preconception planning/smear overread — no urgent referral needed now.
6. Counsel: reassure spontaneous bleeding risk at this level is very low, vaginal delivery and most procedures are safe at >100k, but inform future obstetric, anesthesia, surgical and dental teams; avoid prolonged NSAIDs and excess alcohol; note neuraxial anesthesia generally requires ≥70-80k so needs anesthesiology input in future pregnancy.
7. Return precautions: seek prompt care for new petechiae, purpura, prolonged epistaxis or gum bleeding, heavy menses, hematuria, melena, or bleeding that does not stop with pressure or after procedures.

Severe absolute iron deficiency anemia (Hgb 7.3 g/dL, MCV 67, ferritin <5 ng/mL, low saturation with hypochromic microcytosis) causing fatigue and unresponsive to intermittent iron, most consistent with chronic blood loss or malabsorption rather than hemoglobinopathy.

1. Do not order hemoglobinopathy work-up now (no Hb electrophoresis, alpha/beta gene testing). Iron deficiency fully explains labs; iron deficiency also lowers HbA2 and makes electrophoresis misleading.
2. Obtain focused history and exam: menstrual pattern/menopause status, vaginal bleeding, melena, hematochezia, hematuria, urinary frequency/dysuria, NSAIDs, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, PPIs/antacids, diet/meat intake, weight loss, dyspepsia/dysphagia/diarrhea, blood donation, pica/pagophagia, restless legs, orthostatics, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, vitals with orthostatics.
3. Order: CBC with differential, RDW/RBC count, reticulocyte count, vitamin B12 and folate, CMP, tissue transglutaminase-IgA with total IgA, fecal immunochemical test (FIT), urinalysis with microscopy plus urine culture. Do not repeat iron/ferritin immediately.
4. Replete iron aggressively given Hgb 7.3 and prior failure of intermittent oral iron: refer to hematology/infusion for IV iron, e.g. ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg IV, repeat 750 mg 7-14 days later. If IV unavailable, start ferrous sulfate 325 mg (65 mg elemental) PO daily or every-other-day on empty stomach with vitamin C, separated 2-4 hours from calcium, dairy, tea/coffee, antacids/PPIs, continue 3 months after Hgb normalizes. Counsel dark stools, constipation/nausea are expected.
5. Refer urgently to gastroenterology within 2-4 weeks for bidirectional endoscopy (EGD + colonoscopy) for severe IDA in a 52-year-old without clear cause; do not rely on FIT alone to rule out GI loss. Transfuse only for hemodynamic instability, chest pain, dyspnea at rest, syncope, or active bleeding, not for Hgb 7.3 alone if stable.
6. Evaluate gynecologic and urinary blood loss: gynecology review for perimenopausal menorrhagia/fibroids; quantify bleeding, pelvic exam as indicated. Evaluate recurrent urinary symptoms with UA microscopy for hematuria and culture; do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.
7. Stop chronic intermittent phenazopyridine (Pyridium); limit to max 2 days with UTI antibiotics. It masks hematuria/UTI symptoms and with prolonged use risks methemoglobinemia/hemolysis and renal injury.
8. Follow-up CBC/reticulocytes in 2-4 weeks (expect Hgb rise ~1 g/dL per 2 weeks) and ferritin in 8-12 weeks. If bidirectional endoscopy negative and IDA persists/recurs, pursue small-bowel capsule endoscopy. If microcytosis/RBC elevation persists after ferritin normalized x3 months, then send Hb electrophoresis and consider alpha-thalassemia testing.
9. Return precautions: seek urgent care for chest pain, dyspnea at rest, syncope, palpitations, melena, hematochezia, gross hematuria, heavy vaginal bleeding, or worsening fatigue.

Remote single isolated unprovoked subsegmental PE 3.5 years ago, treated with 3 months apixaban and no recurrence off therapy since, represents a low-risk phenotype where diagnosis is often uncertain and late resumption of anticoagulation offers no proven benefit. In a kidney-transplant recipient with bleeding and drug-interaction risks, harms of restarting indefinite anticoagulation now outweigh benefits.

1. Do not resume indefinite or any routine anticoagulation now, and do not start aspirin as a substitute for VTE prevention; completed 3-month course was appropriate and prolonged event-free interval without therapy argues against recurrence-prone disease.
2. Do not obtain routine surveillance D-dimer, repeat CT pulmonary angiography, bilateral lower-extremity duplex, thrombophilia testing such as factor V Leiden/prothrombin mutation, protein C/S/antithrombin, antiphospholipid panel, or expanded occult-malignancy workup for stable isolated ferritin 1059 ng/mL while asymptomatic with stable CBC/metabolic panel and up-to-date age-appropriate cancer screening.
3. Retrieve prior CT pulmonary angiography report and any lower-extremity duplex from time of PE to confirm true isolated subsegmental defect versus artifact and document in problem list; review with transplant nephrology current creatinine/eGFR, CBC, blood pressure, immunosuppressants, and concomitant antiplatelets, NSAIDs, azoles, or supplements, and avoid NSAIDs and minimize bleeding risks given living alone.
4. Use situational prophylaxis only: for major surgery, trauma, hospitalization with immobility, or prolonged travel/immobilization, coordinate timely pharmacologic prophylaxis per surgical/medical protocol with transplant pharmacy for renal function and calcineurin-inhibitor interactions, plus early ambulation, hydration, and calf-pump exercises; no home modification needed for single-story dwelling.
5. Counsel on VTE symptoms — unilateral leg swelling/pain, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hemoptysis — and that estrogen-containing hormones, smoking, dehydration and prolonged immobility increase risk; continue routine transplant and primary care follow-up, no routine hematology referral unless new event or diagnostic uncertainty.
6. If new suspected DVT/PE occurs, pursue diagnostic bilateral duplex and/or CT pulmonary angiography promptly and, if confirmed, treat with minimum 3 months therapeutic anticoagulation dosed for transplant renal function with interaction check, then reassess extended therapy by bleeding risk. Seek urgent care for leg swelling/pain, breathing difficulty, chest pain, coughing blood, or signs of bleeding.

Substantial HIV exposure from condomless vaginal sex with a recently diagnosed partner, now presenting beyond the 72-hour window when non-occupational PEP is effective and no longer indicated.

1. Do NOT prescribe HIV PEP – no efficacy when started >72 hours after exposure, with risks of toxicity, drug interactions, and resistance without benefit. Document exact exposure date/time, partner ART use/viral load, patient LMP, contraception use, STI symptoms, prior HIV/STI/hepatitis B vaccination history, and acute HIV symptoms.
2. Order baseline testing today: laboratory-based 4th-generation HIV-1/2 Ag/Ab; vaginal NAAT for *N. gonorrhoeae* and *C. trachomatis*; syphilis RPR with reflex treponemal test; hepatitis B surface antigen, surface antibody and core antibody; hepatitis C antibody with reflex RNA; urine hCG. If fever, rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, myalgia/arthralgia within 2-4 weeks of exposure, add plasma HIV RNA for acute infection. If starting PrEP, add serum creatinine/eGFR.
3. Assess pregnancy risk immediately: if unprotected intercourse was ≤120 hours ago and pregnancy not desired, offer emergency contraception – copper IUD within 5 days most effective, or ulipristal acetate 30 mg PO single dose up to 120 hours (preferred if >72 hours or BMI >26), or levonorgestrel 1.5 mg PO single dose within 72 hours. Do not give empiric STI antibiotics; treat only if tests positive.
4. If non-immune to hepatitis B, start vaccination – e.g., Heplisav-B 20 mcg IM at 0 and 1 month – and counsel on condom use with all partners, no blood/organ donation, and use condoms or abstain until 12-week HIV test complete. Encourage partner HIV care, ART adherence/viral suppression, and STI testing.
5. Counsel that baseline HIV test may be negative in window period; schedule repeat 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab at 6 weeks and 12 weeks post-exposure, with 1-2 week follow-up for baseline results. Discuss daily oral PrEP (e.g., tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine) or long-acting PrEP if ongoing HIV risk in this partnership; refer to primary care, sexual health, or infectious disease within 1-2 weeks for PrEP evaluation, not urgent ED/ID.
6. Return precautions: seek prompt care for acute seroconversion symptoms – fever, rash, sore throat, adenopathy, headache, myalgia, vomiting/diarrhea – for HIV RNA testing; also for positive pregnancy test, STI symptoms, or need for intimate-partner violence/sexual health support. If baseline HIV Ag/Ab positive, link urgently to HIV care for HIV RNA, CD4, resistance testing and ART initiation.

Latent TB infection in an asymptomatic IGRA-positive adult with negative chest radiograph from an endemic country, not active TB. Without high-risk progression factors, short-term deferral is safe but treatment is indicated to prevent future reactivation.

1. Confirm latent TB and exclude active TB: review prolonged cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis, lymphadenopathy, prior TB or LTBI treatment, BCG, recent TB contact/travel, country of origin/duration in US, occupation, alcohol/substance use, liver disease, diabetes/CKD/silicosis, HIV risk, immunosuppressive meds (TNF-inhibitor, chronic steroids, chemotherapy, transplant antirejection), and full medication list. Perform focused exam including lungs, nodes, weight. No sputum AFB smear/culture/NAAT, chest CT, repeat IGRA or TST needed now given no symptoms and negative CXR.
2. Assess reactivation and treatment risk: obtain HIV-1/2 4th-generation Ag/Ab, review recent HbA1c/diabetes status, and obtain baseline AST, ALT, and total bilirubin before starting therapy. Review alcohol use and hepatotoxic meds. If HIV-positive, recent close TB contact within 2 years, recent IGRA conversion, immunosuppression, or fibrotic CXR lesions, do not delay — expedite evaluation.
3. Counsel that latent TB is non-infectious: no isolation, work exclusion, or household contact investigation needed; cannot transmit to spouse/children; lifetime reactivation risk ~5-10% without treatment, higher with HIV, diabetes, or immunosuppression.
4. Advise immediate treatment is not required: a 2-3 month delay is acceptable if asymptomatic, CXR negative, and no high-risk features above; document shared decision and specific plan to revisit treatment initiation, and instruct to return sooner if TB symptoms develop. Do not start single- or dual-drug LTBI therapy if active TB symptoms/signs develop — evaluate for active TB first to avoid resistance.
5. When ready, prescribe preferred short-course rifamycin regimen, after active TB excluded and drug interactions reviewed: 12-week once-weekly isoniazid + rifapentine (3HP) — isoniazid 15 mg/kg PO once weekly max 900 mg (typically 900 mg) + rifapentine 900 mg PO once weekly if ≥50 kg (750 mg if 32.1-49.9 kg) for 12 weekly doses, plus pyridoxine 25-50 mg PO with each dose. Alternative if 3HP not tolerated/interacting: rifampin 10 mg/kg PO daily max 600 mg daily for 4 months (120 doses). Avoid alcohol and excess acetaminophen during treatment; counsel rifamycins cause orange urine/tears/sweat, GI upset, rash, flu-like reaction, hepatotoxicity, and reduce efficacy of warfarin, DOACs, anti-epileptics, azoles, hormonal contraception, methadone, and many antiretrovirals — reconcile meds before starting.
6. Arrange nonurgent referral to primary care follow-up in 2-3 months for treatment initiation, or to infectious disease or county health department TB program for education, adherence support, and monthly clinical monitoring during therapy; no routine serial CXR or IGRA to monitor response.
7. Return precautions: seek prompt care for >2-3 weeks cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis, or for drug-induced liver injury — nausea/vomiting, right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, dark urine, unusual fatigue — rash, paresthesias, or vomiting/diarrhea preventing adherence.

Stable mild creatinine elevation with normal cystatin C, bland urinalyses, normotension and no albuminuria suggests normal true GFR with creatinine-based eGFR underestimation from muscle mass/generation rather than CKD, with no features of glomerular or systemic autoimmune disease.

1. Review creatinine trajectory on same assay, BMI/muscle mass, resistance exercise, diet high in cooked meat/protein, creatine monohydrate, whey, NSAIDs, trimethoprim/cimetidine/fibrates, diuretics, volume depletion, smoking, diabetes/hypertension screening, and family history of kidney failure/dialysis, polycystic kidneys, Alport/hearing loss, early hypertension/diabetes; document standardized office BP and 1-week home BP log.
2. Obtain repeat basic metabolic panel with CKD-EPI 2021 eGFRcr, cystatin C with eGFRcys and combined eGFRcr-cys, urinalysis with microscopy, and first-morning spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, drawn euvolemic and 24-48 hours after intense exercise, large meat meal, NSAIDs, or dehydration. Chronicity requires >3 month persistence.
3. Defer repeat renal ultrasound, autoimmune/vasculitis serologies including ANA, RF, ANCA, complements, hepatitis/HIV screening beyond age-appropriate care, and kidney biopsy given normal BP, bland urine, normal cystatin C, prior normal UACR/ultrasound, and non-heritable late-onset RA in grandmother.
4. No nephrology or rheumatology referral now; refer routinely to nephrology if combined eGFRcr-cys <60 mL/min/1.73m2, UACR ≥30 mg/g on repeat, hematuria with proteinuria, active sediment/RBC casts, or sustained hypertension develops.
5. Counsel to maintain hydration, avoid NSAIDs/aminoglycosides if possible, avoid creatine loading and inform lab of supplements, and that isolated 0.1-0.2 mg/dL creatinine fluctuation is often assay/muscle/diet related when cystatin C is normal; no ACE inhibitor, immunosuppression, or antibiotics indicated.
6. Recheck BMP/eGFRcr-cys, UA, UACR and BP in 3-6 months, then annually if stable; seek sooner for gross hematuria, foamy urine, leg/periorbital edema, oliguria, dyspnea, chest pain, severe headache, or BP >140/90.

Prior severe C. difficile requiring FMT increases vigilance for recurrence, but persistent loose non-watery stool without ≥3 watery stools/day, cramps, fever, or leukocytosis after low-risk azithromycin is low probability for active CDI and high risk for false-positive colonization.

1. Do not order C. difficile testing now and do not screen formed or non-watery stool. Testing without a diarrheal syndrome, especially NAAT alone in a post-FMT patient, detects colonization and leads to unnecessary treatment and microbiome disruption.
2. Document stool burden to guide future decisions: number of unformed stools (Bristol 6-7, takes shape of container) per 24 hours, laxatives, magnesium/antacids, new foods, PPIs, NSAIDs, and pneumonia course - fever, cough, dyspnea improving on azithromycin. Hold laxatives/stool softeners if present. No labs, stool panel, CT, or colonoscopy now.
3. Do not start empiric vancomycin, fidaxomicin, or metronidazole, and do not stop azithromycin early for this bowel change alone. Manage supportively with oral hydration; avoid loperamide, probiotics, and new PPIs/antibiotics unless clearly indicated.
4. Test conditionally only if new-onset unexplained ≥3 unformed/watery stools in 24 hours, especially with crampy abdominal pain, fever, leukocytosis, or recurrent bloody stools: send one unformed stool sample off laxatives for GDH antigen plus toxin A/B EIA with reflex to NAAT (2-step algorithm). Do not repeat negatives or test to confirm cure.
5. Counsel on soap-and-water hand hygiene if diarrhea worsens, avoidance of unnecessary antibiotics, and that transient bloody loose stools that have fully resolved without anemia, weight loss, or recurrent bleeding do not require urgent GI evaluation. Verify age-appropriate colorectal cancer screening is up to date at routine visit.
6. Follow up in primary care in 1-2 weeks if loose stools persist, sooner if criteria in #4 develop. Seek urgent care for: ≥3 watery stools/day for >24-48h, fever, worsening abdominal pain/tenderness, recurrent gross blood, vomiting/dehydration, dizziness, reduced urine, or worsening pneumonia symptoms. If those develop, evaluate for CDI and refer urgently to GI/ID; otherwise no specialty referral.

Dilute urine with persistent frequency/nocturia and normal CMP/A1c suggests hypotonic polyuria — central vs nephrogenic diabetes insipidus vs primary polydipsia vs low solute intake — rather than bacterial UTI or hyperglycemic diuresis.

1. Quantify polyuria with 3-day frequency-volume diary recording all fluid intake type/volume, voided volumes and times, nocturnal vs 24-hour urine volume, caffeine/alcohol use, sleep and snoring: polyuria defined as >3 L/day or >50 mL/kg/day; nocturnal polyuria as >33% of 24-hour volume at this age.
2. Obtain paired morning serum osmolality, serum sodium, and first-morning urine osmolality with urine specific gravity, plus 24-hour urine collection for volume, creatinine, osmolality, sodium and potassium to calculate total solute excretion; excretion <600-800 mOsm/day suggests low protein/salt intake/beer potomania rather than DI.
3. Take focused history and exam: thirst/polydipsia onset, daily water intake, diet protein/salt and alcohol/beer intake, weight change, medications/supplements — lithium, diuretics, SGLT2 inhibitors, anticholinergics — head trauma, pituitary surgery/tumor, meningitis, family history of DI, psychiatric history, smoking/cannabis, sexual history, dysuria/discharge/pelvic pain, snoring/apnea, edema, plus vitals, weight, and prostate/genital exam; do not repeat CMP/A1c if recently normal.
4. Rule out persistent urinary infection/LUTS without empiric retreatment: urinalysis with microscopy and reflex urine culture, nucleic acid amplification test for Neisseria gonorrhoeae/Chlamydia trachomatis if at risk or with discharge/dysuria, and bladder-scan post-void residual; do not prescribe antibiotics, antimuscarinics, desmopressin, or fluid restriction at this stage.
5. If labs show hypotonic polyuria — e.g., 24-hour volume >3 L with urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg, especially with serum sodium >142 mEq/L or serum osmolality >295 mOsm/kg — refer to endocrinology/nephrology for supervised water-deprivation test with copeptin measurement; if central DI confirmed or suspected from pituitary history, hyperprolactinemia, or visual field defect, obtain MRI sella with contrast via endocrinology; if polyuria excluded and storage symptoms persist, refer to urology in 4-6 weeks.
6. Counsel to maintain ad lib fluids until evaluated, avoid unsupervised water deprivation or overdrinking, limit caffeine/alcohol excess, and bring medication list and diary to 1-2 week follow-up; seek sooner for fever, vomiting/diarrhea, inability to keep up with thirst, severe dizziness, confusion, or very low urine output suggesting hypernatremic dehydration.

Incidental renal infarct in a 60-year-old with ovarian cancer history most likely reflects cardioembolism, aortic/renal atherosclerosis, or cancer-associated hypercoagulability. Maternal RA alone without patient arthritis, rash, pulmonary-renal or systemic features does not suggest vasculitis or RA-related renal disease.

1. Obtain focused history and exam: atrial fibrillation/palpitations/syncope, murmur, endocarditis features/fever, recent MI, heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, dyslipidemia, claudication, prior stroke/TIA or peripheral embolus, active cancer status/recent chemotherapy/hormonal therapy, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use and bleeding risk, plus vitals with bilateral arm BP, pulse rhythm, cardiac murmur, lung, abdominal bruits, livedo, digital ischemia, neurologic deficits, and edema.
2. Evaluate for cardioembolic source promptly: 12-lead ECG now, transthoracic echocardiogram within 1-2 weeks to assess LV thrombus, valves/vegetations, ejection fraction and shunt, and 14-day ambulatory patch monitor if ECG and telemetry negative and no clear atherosclerotic/aortic source.
3. Obtain CT angiography of abdomen/pelvis with arterial phase to confirm infarct, assess renal artery stenosis/dissection/fibromuscular dysplasia, and aortic atheroma/aneurysm/thrombus; do not order carotid Doppler, lower-extremity venous Doppler, or renal biopsy without specific indication.
4. Check kidney impact and vascular risk: repeat basic metabolic panel/eGFR in 7 days then in 1 month, urinalysis with microscopy plus spot urine protein/creatinine ratio, CBC, fasting lipid panel, and hemoglobin A1c; institute home BP monitoring twice daily for 2 weeks then per nephrology.
5. Do not order RF, anti-CCP, ANA, ANCA, complement, cryoglobulins, or inherited thrombophilia panel (Factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, protein C/S/antithrombin) based solely on maternal RA or single infarct; reserve lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG/IgM and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I IgG/IgM and hematology input for cryptogenic arterial thrombosis after cardiac/vascular evaluation or if recurrent thrombosis, livedo, pregnancy loss, or prolonged aPTT.
6. Refer urgently to cardiology within 1 week and nephrology within 2 weeks, and update oncology on infarct to review cancer activity, ongoing surveillance, and prothrombotic therapy vs bleeding risk; defer antithrombotic choice to cardiology/nephrology — if AF/LV thrombus confirmed, anticoagulation after bleeding assessment, if atherosclerotic/aortic plaque without cardioembolism, antiplatelet plus high-intensity statin (e.g., atorvastatin 40-80 mg daily if eligible) — avoid starting empiric anticoagulation plus antiplatelet or NSAIDs/aminoglycosides/iodinated contrast without indication.
7. Counsel that small infarct with normal creatinine can still cause delayed hypertension, proteinuria, and CKD, and recurrent embolism risk depends on cause; seek urgent care for worsening flank/abdominal pain, gross hematuria, oliguria/anuria, severe headache, BP >180/120, chest pain, palpitations/syncope, focal weakness/speech change, or cold/painful limb.

High-risk TIA with transient right hemiparesis, ABCD2 5, and multiple vascular risk factors with negative MRI 8 days ago — high short-term recurrent stroke risk requiring urgent completion of secondary prevention workup; DAPT started now is outside the proven <24-hour window.

1. Obtain urgent CTA head and neck with contrast today and urgent neurology/stroke clinic within 24-48 hours; send to ED immediately if imaging unavailable outpatient, new deficits, or critical stenosis found.
2. Stop clopidogrel 75 mg — index event ~8 days ago is beyond the 24-hour window where aspirin + clopidogrel x21 days reduces recurrence; continue aspirin 81 mg daily alone; confirm plan urgently with neurology, and reload DAPT only if new high-risk TIA/minor stroke occurs per neurology.
3. Start high-intensity statin now, e.g., atorvastatin 40 mg daily, titrate to 80 mg as tolerated, regardless of baseline LDL; recheck fasting lipid panel and ALT in 4-12 weeks; counsel on muscle pain/tenderness and bleeding risk with aspirin.
4. Complete cardiac and metabolic workup: 12-lead ECG today, continue 7-day Zio patch as ordered with plan for rapid review; obtain hemoglobin A1c, fasting lipid panel, CBC, basic metabolic panel, and bilateral office BP if not current; obtain transthoracic echocardiogram with bubble only if no large-vessel disease or atrial fibrillation found, or if murmur, HF, or suspected cardioembolism.
5. Optimize long-term vascular risk without acute over-lowering: continue current antihypertensives/diabetes meds targeting BP <130/80 long-term and individualized A1c goal for 77-year-old; counsel on Mediterranean diet, daily walking as tolerated, smoking cessation and alcohol limits if applicable, and medication adherence.
6. If CTA shows symptomatic 70-99% left internal carotid stenosis, refer emergently to vascular surgery/neurointervention for carotid endarterectomy/stenting within 14 days; if Zio/ECG shows atrial fibrillation/flutter, stop antiplatelet, start anticoagulation per cardiology/neurology and refer to cardiology promptly.
7. No repeat brain MRI/CT, EEG, hypercoagulable panel, or BRCA/cancer workup for mother’s postmenopausal breast cancer at age 72; continue age-appropriate screening only.
8. Follow up in primary care in 1-2 weeks for BP, A1c/lipids, statin tolerance, Zio and CTA results, and neurology coordination; advise no driving until cleared by neurology.
9. Return precautions: call 911 for recurrent weakness, facial droop, speech change, vision loss, severe headache, chest pain, or signs of bleeding on aspirin.

**Clinical assessment:** High-frequency episodic migraine without aura with functional impairment and chronification over 18 months. Typical phenotype and duration with photophobia/nausea and no focal deficits favors primary migraine; remote repetitive TBI does not establish secondary headache.

1. Complete focused assessment now: vitals including BP/HR, full neurologic exam including fundoscopy, screen for SNOOP red flags, frequency of aspirin/ibuprofen use, caffeine/alcohol/sleep/stress triggers, depression/anxiety, sleep apnea, and timing/sequelae of TBIs with post-concussive cognitive/mood symptoms; start headache diary documenting frequency, duration, laterality, associated symptoms, triggers, acute-med use and response.
2. Defer routine neuroimaging and labs/EEG at this time given typical migraine phenotype and normal exam without red flags; if exam abnormal, strictly fixed unilateral pain, thunderclap onset, new focal deficit, seizure, altered consciousness, fever/meningismus, papilledema, or major pattern change, obtain MRI brain without contrast, with CT head without contrast only if emergent or MRI unavailable/contraindicated.
3. Stop concurrent aspirin plus ibuprofen; prescribe migraine-specific abortive: sumatriptan 100 mg PO at headache onset, may repeat once after 2 hours if incomplete relief, max 200 mg/24 hours, limit to <10 days/month, after screening for coronary disease, stroke, peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic migraine, and use of MAOIs/ergots; advise chest tightness, flushing, paresthesias, and avoid driving if sedated, and avoid opioids, butalbital, and daily NSAIDs.
4. Initiate preventive therapy given 8-12 headache days/month with work impairment: propranolol extended-release 80 mg PO daily, titrate to 120-240 mg daily as tolerated by HR/BP, trial for 2-3 months to assess benefit, after screening for asthma/COPD, bradycardia/heart block, hypotension, depression, and diabetes; counsel fatigue, dizziness, bradycardia, sexual dysfunction, and do not stop abruptly.
5. Counsel on medication-overuse risk: limit triptans to <10 days/month and NSAIDs to <15 days/month, take NSAIDs only intermittently with food; maintain regular sleep, hydration, aerobic exercise, limit caffeine and alcohol, stress management; advise avoidance of further head impacts, helmet use, no return-to-contact sport while symptomatic, and discuss expected course with 4-8 weeks for preventive benefit.
6. Refer to neurology routinely, non-urgent within 2-3 months, for diagnostic confirmation and longitudinal preventive management given progression, high frequency, and repetitive TBI history; if inadequate response or intolerance after adequate trial, neurology to consider alternative preventive such as amitriptyline, topiramate with cognitive monitoring, or CGRP-targeted therapy.
7. Follow up in primary care in 4-6 weeks to review diary, disability, acute-med use, HR/BP, tolerability and adherence; seek urgent care sooner for thunderclap worst-ever headache, new weakness/numbness, speech/vision change, confusion, seizure, fever with neck stiffness, head trauma, headache >72 hours unresponsive to abortive, or chest pain/neurologic symptoms after triptan.

Persistent confusion with delusions/paranoia 3 months after CABG-associated delirium, now oriented with normal exam and negative CT and no prior dementia/psychosis, suggests unmasked major neurocognitive disorder, recurrent/persistent delirium, or new medical/psychiatric cause requiring systematic cognitive, safety, and reversible-cause evaluation.

1. Perform structured cognitive-functional assessment with informant: compare to pre-CABG baseline, review onset/course/fluctuation, ADLs/IADLs, living supervision, driving, and decision-making; administer MoCA, Confusion Assessment Method for delirium, PHQ-9 for depression, and assess delusion/paranoia content, hallucinations, suicidal/homicidal/violent ideation, agitation, and access to weapons.
2. Complete medication, supplement, and substance review: prescription, OTC, antihistamines, sleep aids, muscle relaxants, opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, recent anesthesia/sedatives, alcohol, cannabis, and withdrawal; hold/discontinue nonessential sedating/anticholinergic agents, do not start empiric antipsychotic, benzodiazepine, or cholinesterase inhibitor.
3. Obtain focused vitals including orthostatics and pulse oximetry, ECG for atrial fibrillation/ischemia, and review CABG course, cardiopulmonary status, infection, pain, sleep, constipation, urinary retention, hydration, and sensory impairment.
4. Order targeted reversible-cause labs: CBC, basic metabolic panel with calcium and magnesium, hepatic panel, TSH with reflex to free T4, and vitamin B12; add urinalysis, blood cultures, or toxicology only if fever, urinary symptoms, leukocytosis, or suspected exposure.
5. Order MRI brain without contrast to evaluate for post-CABG embolic infarcts, small-vessel disease, subdural collection, or normal-pressure hydrocephalus not seen on noncontrast CT; do not repeat head CT, and reserve MRA/CTA, EEG, lumbar puncture, or PET for focal deficits, atrial fibrillation/stroke pattern on MRI, seizure-like fluctuations, or focal neurologic signs.
6. Refer promptly to neurology in 2-4 weeks with formal neuropsychological testing in 4-6 weeks for persistent deficit, and to geriatric psychiatry/psychiatry within 1-2 weeks for late-onset delusions/paranoia; send to ED urgently if unsafe, highly agitated, or suicidal/homicidal.
7. Counsel to provide 24-hour supervision, suspend driving and high-risk activities until cleared, ensure sleep, hydration, glasses/hearing aids, and cardiac medication adherence, and schedule primary care follow-up in 1-2 weeks to review results; if MRI shows infarct initiate stroke secondary prevention, if labs abnormal correct cause and reassess cognition.
8. Return precautions: seek urgent care for worsening confusion, agitation, new weakness, speech change, syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, fever, falls, or any intent to harm self or others.

New RLL tree-in-bud micronodularity with bronchial wall thickening and mucus plugging shortly after a self-limited cough in a now asymptomatic 71-year-old most likely represents resolving infectious bronchiolitis rather than active mycobacterial disease, chronic aspiration, or malignancy.

1. Do not start empiric antibiotics, systemic steroids, or obtain sputum bacterial/AFB cultures, QuantiFERON-TB Gold, PET-CT, bronchoscopy, or biopsy now given absence of current respiratory or systemic symptoms.
2. Take focused interval history and exam: TB contacts, travel/birthplace, hot-tub/sauna/soil/dust exposure, sick contacts, dysphagia, choking, reflux, dysphonia, neurologic disease, alcohol/sedative use, asthma/wheezing/atopy, prior eosinophil counts/trends and meds/supplements/travel/parasite risks, glycemic control and vaccination status; record vitals, SpO2, and lung exam.
3. Obtain repeat noncontrast thin-section chest CT (low-dose technique if adequate) in 3 months to document resolution; if resolved, resume routine annual low-dose CT for lung cancer screening with no further workup for this finding.
4. If follow-up CT shows persistence, progression, bronchiectasis/cavitation, or if he develops persistent cough >2-3 weeks, purulent sputum, hemoptysis, fever, weight loss or night sweats, refer non-urgently to pulmonology within 2-4 weeks for sputum bacterial culture and AFB smear plus mycobacterial culture x3 on separate days, QuantiFERON-TB Gold if risk factors, and given chronic eosinophilia plus plugging, CBC with differential, total serum IgE, and Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE and IgG for ABPA/eosinophilic disease.
5. Counsel that this pattern commonly follows viral or self-limited bacterial bronchiolitis and usually resolves without treatment, reinforce continued smoking abstinence and good glycemic control, and ensure age-appropriate respiratory vaccines per CDC (annual influenza, pneumococcal, updated COVID-19).
6. Return precautions: seek prompt care for fever, worsening/persistent cough, increased or bloody sputum, dyspnea, chest pain, weight loss, or night sweats.

Recurrent prolonged productive cough after viral illnesses with normal exam and chest X-ray suggests post-viral airway inflammation with possible underlying chronic bronchitis, upper airway cough syndrome, or occult bronchiectasis rather than recurrent acute bacterial infection requiring antibiotics.

1. Do not continue empiric azithromycin for each episode; transient improvement likely reflects natural resolution and anti-inflammatory effect, not bacterial cure, and repeated use in a 71-year-old increases QT arrhythmia, hearing loss, C. difficile, drug interactions, and resistance without preventing recurrence.
2. Obtain focused history at next visit: smoking pack-years and vaping/biomass/occupational exposures, ACE-inhibitor use, sputum color/volume/duration, nasal congestion/post-nasal drip/sinus pressure, dyspnea/wheeze, fever, hemoptysis, weight loss, reflux/heartburn/regurgitation, and review pending spirometry with bronchodilator response.
3. Do not escalate acid suppression for cough alone; PPIs already tried without relief, and productive post-viral cough is atypical for GERD — continue famotidine for GERD symptoms only.
4. During next productive episode, obtain expectorated sputum Gram stain and bacterial culture with sensitivities before any antibiotic, and reserve antibiotics for increased dyspnea plus increased sputum volume plus increased purulence, fever, or clinical deterioration — do not treat clear/white sputum or isolated cough empirically.
5. Obtain high-resolution CT chest without contrast to evaluate for bronchiectasis given yearly >4-week productive episodes despite normal X-ray; if CT confirms bronchiectasis, refer to pulmonology routinely in 4-6 weeks for airway clearance planning and sputum mycobacterial workup rather than starting chronic macrolide in primary care.
6. Ensure age-appropriate respiratory prevention: annual inactivated influenza, pneumococcal, RSV, and updated COVID-19 vaccines per CDC, plus hand hygiene and avoidance of smoke/irritants; counsel that post-viral cough often lasts 3-8 weeks and does not require antibiotics.
7. Follow up to review PFTs and episode frequency in 4-6 weeks, sooner if purulent exacerbation; refer to ENT routinely if chronic nasal symptoms/post-nasal drip, and to pulmonology if obstruction on PFTs, CT abnormality, or >2 purulent exacerbations/year.
8. Return precautions: seek urgent care for hemoptysis, fever >101F persisting >3 days, worsening dyspnea/wheeze, chest pain, or sputum becoming frankly purulent with increased volume.

Active endobronchial mycobacterial infection, likely tuberculosis reactivation given prior positive QuantiFERON without documented treatment plus prolonged steroids, rather than checkpoint pneumonitis relapse. Tree-in-bud bronchial disease is atypical for immune-related pneumonitis and empiric steroids risk dissemination.

1. Do not restart prednisone or other systemic corticosteroids until active tuberculosis is ruled out.
2. Manage as suspected active pulmonary TB: outpatient airborne precautions with surgical mask on patient and N95 for contacts, stay home and avoid close contacts especially infants and immunocompromised, single airborne room if presenting to clinic/ED, and notify infection control and local health department per suspect-TB protocol.
3. Hold further checkpoint immunotherapy pending evaluation and coordinate with oncology; do not treat for presumed pneumonitis.
4. Clarify history: prior latent TB treatment completion 5 years ago, prior sputum AFB/NAAT results, TB exposures, contacts, travel, BCG, HIV risks, diabetes, smoking, known bronchiectasis, and compare current CT to prior chest CTs.
5. Obtain 3 expectorated sputum samples, induced if needed, each for AFB smear, M. tuberculosis NAAT with Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, and mycobacterial culture, plus bacterial sputum culture; obtain baseline CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel with LFTs, hemoglobin A1c, and HIV-1/2 Ag/Ab combo assay.
6. If unable to expectorate or smear/NAAT negative but suspicion remains, obtain urgent pulmonology referral within 1 week for bronchoscopy with BAL for AFB smear, MTB NAAT, mycobacterial, bacterial and fungal cultures, and cytology.
7. Avoid empiric fluoroquinolones, macrolides, or other antibiotics before mycobacterial sampling unless septic; defer empiric anti-mycobacterial therapy to infectious disease.
8. Obtain urgent infectious disease referral within days for TB versus nontuberculous mycobacteria management and contact investigation guidance.
9. If active MTB confirmed, ID and public health to direct weight-based multidrug therapy and contact tracing; if NTM confirmed, ID/pulmonology to direct guideline-based therapy; if infection is fully excluded and immune pneumonitis is reconsidered, pulmonology/oncology to direct any future steroid course with Pneumocystis prophylaxis and metabolic monitoring.
10. Return precautions: seek urgent care for worsening dyspnea, hypoxia, fever, hemoptysis, chest pain, night sweats or weight loss.
